Synthesis_Procedure: The standard ceramic method is used to prepare M-type hexagonal ferrite samples with chemical formula Ba0.5Sr0.5CoxWxFe(12−2x)O19 (x = 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8 and 1.0) [16]. AR grade of BaCo3 (99.99% purity, E-Merck, Germany), SrCo3 (99.99% purity, E-Merck, Germany), CoCO3 (99.99% purity, E-Merck, Germany), WO2 (99.99% purity, E-Merck, Germany) and Fe2O3 (99.99% purity, E-Merck, Germany) were used as starting materials. The stoichiometric amount of different chemical reagents of compositions was grounded in an agate pestle and mortar in the distilled water for 8 h. The ground mixed powders were pre-sintered at 1000 °C for 10 h in microcontroller programmed an electric furnace and recovered powders were reground under the same conditions in order to produce fine powder material. The sieving of powders was carried out with sieves of mesh size 220 B.S.S. After adding polyvinyl alcohol (PVA) in fine powder; pellets of each composition were prepared, using a hydraulic press under a uniaxial pressure of 75 kN/m2. The final sintering of pellets was carried out at 1150 °C for 15 h. The heating and cooling rates of an electric furnace were set to ±5 °C.

The ground mixed powders were pre-sintered at 1000 °C for 10 h in microcontroller programmed an electric furnace and recovered powders were reground under the same conditions in order to produce fine powder material. The sieving of powders was carried out with sieves of mesh size 220 B.S.S. After adding polyvinyl alcohol (PVA) in fine powder; pellets of each composition were prepared, using a hydraulic press under a uniaxial pressure of 75 kN/m2. The Ba0.5Sr0.5-xGdxFe12.0-xZnxO19 (0.0 ≤ x ≤ 0.4) hexaferrites were synthesized by sol-gel auto-combustion method. All the precursors were of analytical grade, weighed according to the stoichiometric calculations. A stoichiometric mixture solution was prepared by dissolving Ba(NO3)2, Sr(NO3)2, Fe(NO3)3·9H2O, Gd(NO3)3·6H2O, Zn(NO3)3·6H2O and C6H8O7 acid in deionized water. The mole ratio of total metal ions to citric acid was 1:1. NH4OH solution was then added to keep the pH value of the solution at 7. The solution was evaporated gently at 80 °C under a constant stirring until the solution appeared to be more viscous with the final form of a brownish gel. As the temperature was steadily increasing up to 150 °C and the gel started burning out. After this, the powders were grinded in an agate mortar and pestle. In order to achieve M-type hexaferrite phase, the crushed powders were annealed in a muffle furnace at temperature of 1200 °C for 2 h.

Chemicals used in the synthesis of samples were Fe(NO3)3·9H2O (Panreac Quimica SA, 98%), Sr(NO3)2 (Fluka, ≥99%), ZrOCl2·4H2O (BDH, 96%), Mn(CH3 COO)2·4H2O (Merck, 98%) and NaOH (Fluka, ≥97%). The strontium hexaferrite samples substituted with Zr–Mn and having nominal composition SrZrxMnxFe12−2xO19 (where x = 0.0–0.8) were prepared by a chemical co-precipitation method [10] keeping the molar ratio (Fe/Sr = 11). The theoretical ratio of Fe/Sr = 12.0 as in chemical formula is obtained when the Fe/Sr ratio is kept 11.0. This is due to the higher solubility of Fe than that of Sr and it is necessary to keep the concentration of strontium slightly higher to obtain the pure hexagonal phase. The 2 M solution of NaOH was used as precipitating agent. The detail of experiment can be found in Ref. [17]. The precipitates were annealed at temperature of 1193 K for 1 h to obtain the single phase.

The chemicals used in the synthesis of strontium hexaferrite and its Bi–Cr substituted derivatives were Fe(NO3)3·9H2O (Riedel-dehaem, 97%), Bi(NO3)3·5H2O (Sigma, 98%), Sr(NO3)2 (Harris chemical, 99.99%), Cr(NO3)3·9H2O (Merck, 99.99%), HNO3 (Merck, 65%), ethylene glycol (Fluka, 99%) and NH3 (Merck, 35%). These chemicals were used as such without further treatment. The strontium hexaferrite with nominal composition SrFe12 − xBixCrxO19 (where x =0.0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8, 1) was prepared by the sol–gel method. The solutions of required molarities for the required metal salts were prepared by dissolving the stoichiometric amounts in deionized water. Bismuth nitrate is insoluble in water and was dissolved in minimum volume of nitric acid and then diluted to required volume with deionized water. The solutions were mixed in a 500 mL beaker and stirred using magnetic stirrer with controlled thermostat. The stoichiometric amount of ethylene glycol was added as a chelating agent. The solution mixture was heated up to 60 °C with continuous stirring on a hot plate. The 2.0 M ammonium hydroxide was added drop wise to adjust pH to 7 and then the solution was evaporated slowly by heating at 80 °C with continuous stirring. The sol is transformed into a brown gel after the water evaporation. The gel was then burned by heating at 300 °C to obtain the powder which was finally annealed at 950 °C for 5 h in an electric furnace (VULCAN™ A550).
Journal: Journal of Magnetism and Magnetic Materials

Synthesis_Procedure: To prepare MFe12O19 (M = Ba, Pb, Sr) hexaferrites, Ba(NO3)2⋅4H2O, Pb(NO3)2⋅4H2O, Sr(NO3)2, Fe(NO3)3⋅9H2O, ammonia (NH3), and citric acid (C6H8O7.H2O) as raw materials were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich and used without further purification. For the synthesis of single-phase hexaferrites by the citrate-nitrate method, firstly, we investigated the effect of the synthesis parameters, such as the iron-to-barium molar ratio (10, 11, and 12), the nitrate-tocitrate ratio (0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2, 4, and 6), and the heating temperature (750, 850, and 950 °C) at pH 7 for the formation reaction of pure-phase BaFe12O19. The results (not included here) showed that pure-phase BaFe12O19 powders can be obtained through the citrate-nitrate process with an iron-to-barium molar ratio of 11, a nitrate-to-citrate ratio of 1.5, and a heating temperature of 850 °C at pH 7. However, the pH has too much of an effect on the morphology, decreasing the optimum calcination temperature and the formation of single-phase hexaferrites. The literature shows that the pH can be considered as the key factor for controlling the ferrite nanostructure, and optimal physical properties are found at pH 7 [35,36]. Therefore, to prepare MFe12O19 (M = Ba, Pb, Sr) hexaferrites, specified amounts of the raw materials, Ba(NO3)2⋅4H2O, Pb (NO3)2⋅4H2O, Sr(NO3)2, Fe(NO3)3⋅9H2O, and citric acid, were completely dissolved in the minimum amount of deionized water (solution) with a nitrate-to-citrate molar ratio of 1.5:1. Then ammonia (NH3) was added to adjust the pH to 7 under stirring. The resulting solution was heated in an oil bath kept at 200 °C for 24 h to evaporate water. The resulting wet gels of high viscosity were then placed in an oven at 200 °C for 2 h to form a dry gel. The powders obtained were put in a furnace at 850 °C for 4 h.
Journal: Journal of Physics and Chemistry of Solids

Synthesis_Procedure: The chemicals used in this work are Fe(NO3)3·9H2O (97% Riedel Dehaen), CaCl2·2H2O (99% Merck), Sr(NO3)3 (99%Fluka), ZrOCl2·8H2O(98% Merck), CuCl2·2H2O(99% Merck) and ammonia solution (33% Merck). Zirconium and copper doped M-type Sr–Ca hexaferrites with composition Sr0.5Ca0.5Fe12−2xZrxCuxO19 (x = 0.0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8) have been synthesized by chemical co-precipitation method. The required amounts of the metal salts were dissolved in deionized water in each 250 ml measuring flask to prepare the solutions. All these solutions were then homogenously mixed in a 2000 ml beaker by using hot plate with magnetic stirrer. After half an hour, 4.0 M ammonia solution (precipitating agent) was started to add drop wise in the reaction mixture and the pH of the reaction mixture was maintained between 10 and 11 to achieve the maximum precipitation. Then the solution was stirred at 343 K for 3 h. The resulted precipitates were washed by deionized water to take out their water soluble impurities i.e. nitrates and chlorides, etc. and dried in an electric oven at 373 K for 48 h. The dried precursors were annealed at 1273 K for 6 h in a furnace (VULCAN™ A-550) to obtain the single phase M-type hexagonal structure of the compounds.

They were dissolved in distilled water with citric acid. The nominal molar ratio of the mixed solutions were 1:5 of [total amount of metals]:[citric acid]. The obtained precursors were ground with an alumina mortar and compacted by uniaxial pressing into disk specimens, 20 mm in diameter × 1 mm thick, and then heated at a temperature range between 1073 and 1223 K for 24 h in air.

Synthesis_Procedure: All chemicals (acquired from Sigma-Aldrich and Vetec) used to synthesize SrFe12-xSmxO19 (0≤x≤0.15) powders were of high purity (> 99.9%) and were used without further purification. During a typical synthesis, Sr(NO3)2 and Fe(NO3)3.9H2O were weighed stoichiometrically and then completely dissolved in filtered (Unifil 80 g/cm2) coconut water (Cocos mucifera), [38]. In the synthesis, Fe3+ : Sr2+ molar ratio was fixed at 12:1. The system remained under agitation until it achieved complete homogenization. Upon completion, the initial solution had its pH adjusted to 5.0 through the addition of ammonium hydroxide at 30%. We maintained the agitation until the formation of the sol. Afterwards, we heated the sol up to 100 °C and kept on constant temperature for 24 h to dehydrate. The result was a very porous and low-density solid material (xerogel). This material was heated at 500 °C for 2 hours (with a heating and cooling rate of 2 °C/min) to decompose the initial salts and remove the organic phase. After cooling, the material was homogenized and calcined at 1000 °C for 2h in open atmosphere with a heating and cooling rate of 2 °C/min. The production of the doped material followed the same procedure, but the strontium salt Sr(NO3)2 was mixed to the samarium salt (Sm(NO3)3.6H2O) in the following ratios: 5%; 10% and 15%.

The chemical precursors used for these experiments are Fe(NO3)3·9H2O, Sr(NO3)2 , Pr(NO3)3·6H2O and NaOH. The precursors were weighted according to different Pr3+ /Sr2+ ratios (n = Pr3+ /Sr3+ ), where n was varied between 1/16 and 1/4, while Sr2+ /Fe3+ and [NO3 − ]/[OH− ] ratios were fixed at 1/8 and 1/2, respectively. A water solution containing Sr2+ , Fe3+ and Pr3+ ions was poured into the solution of NaOH. Aqueous suspensions containing the precipitated products were stirred at 1000 rpm and heated to 220 °C for 3 h in an autoclave at a pressure of 25 bar [13]. The resultant particles were carefully washed and filtered using deionised water, and then dried overnight at 80 °C. In order to homogenise the materials and improve the magnetic properties, the as-synthesised particles were then calcined at temperatures from 1000 to 1250 °C for 2 h in air.

The standard ceramic method is used to prepare M-type hexagonal ferrite samples with compositions Ba0.5Sr0.5CoxAlxFe(12−2x)O19 (x = 0.0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8 and 1.0) [13]. AR grade of BaCo3 (Sigma-Aldrich 99.98% pure), SrCo3 (Sigma-Aldrich 99.98%), CoCO3 (Sigma-Aldrich 99.98% pure), Al2O3 (Sigma-Aldrich 99.98% pure), Fe2O3 (Sigma-Aldrich 99.98% pure) used as starting materials. The stoichiometric amount of different chemical reagents of compositions was grounded in an agate pestle and mortar in the distilled water for 8 h and ground mixed powders were then presintered at 1000 °C for 10 h in an electric furnace and obtained powders were reground under the same conditions in order to produce fine material. The sieving of powders was carried out with sieves of mesh size 220 B.S.S. and powders were pressed into pellets using a hydraulic press under an uniaxial pressure of 75 kN/m2 and the final sintering of pellets was carried out at 1250 °C for 20 h, followed by furnace cooling to room temperature in order to increase the density of prepared material and to obtain desired product of Ba0.5Sr0.5CoxAlxFe(12−2x)O19 (x = 0.0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8 and 1.0) hexagonal ferrite powders. The heating and cooling rates were set to ±5 °C.

The chemicals used for the preparation of the samples were Ba(NO3)2 (99%, Sigma Aldrich), Sr(NO3)2·4H2O (98%, Sigma Aldrich), and FeCl3·9H2O (97%, Sigma Aldrich), Al(NO3)3 4H2O (98%, Sigma Aldrich) and Tb2O3 (99%, Sigma Aldrich). The stock solution of each chemical in de-ionized water was prepared in a 100 ml beaker by using stoichiometric amounts of the respective metal salts and stirred for 15 min. The solutions of the required concentrations were mixed in a 1000 ml Pyrex beaker and heated at a constant temperature of 80 °C under constant stirring on a hot plate with magnetic stirrer. The citric acid was added to the metal solution and kept the molar ratio between metal and citric acid 1:1.5. Ammonia solution was added to adjust the pH value to 7.0. The solution was slowly evaporated at 80 °C until a viscous gel is formed. The temperature of the hot plate magnetic stirrer was increased up to about 200 °C for the ignition of the gel. The dried gel burnt in a self-propagating combustion manner until all of it was completely burnt out as brown colored fluffy powders. The gel was heated at 500 °C for 4 h to decompose the organic precursor in the digitally controlled microwave oven ‘‘Wise Ven Fuzy Control System’’. The powders were pressed into pellets of size (3.5 mm thickness and 8 mm diameter) under a force of 30 kN by using the Paul Otto Webber hydraulic press. The sintering of the powders and pellets was carried out simultaneously at 1100 °C for 5 h in a furnace ‘‘Hobersal model HD-230’’ to convert it into hexagonal phase. The synthesis steps are shown in Fig. 1.

The chemical precursors used for these experiments are Fe(NO3)3·9H2O, Sr(NO3)2 , La(NO3)3 ·xH2O, and NaOH. An aqueous water solution containing Sr2+ , Fe3+ and Nd3+ was poured into a solution of NaOH. Aqueous suspensions containing the precipitated products were stirred at 1000 rpm and heated to 220 °C for 3 h in an autoclave at a pressure of 25 bar. The resultant particles were carefully washed and filtered using deionised water, and then dried overnight at 80 °C. In order to homogenise the materials and improve the magnetic properties, the as-synthesised particles were then calcined at temperatures from 1000 to 1300 °C for 2 h in air.

Sr–Nd–Co hexagonal ferrites were prepared by sol–gel-autocombustion method. According to Sr1−xNdxFe12−xCoxO19 (x = 0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4), stoichiometric amounts of strontium nitrate, cobalt nitrate, neodymium nitrate, and iron nitrate were dissolved in deionized water, and then the proper amount of citric acid was added to complex the metal ions completely. The molar ration of citric acid and NO3 ions was controlled as 1:1. The pH value of the sol was adjusted to 6.0 using ammonia solution (25 wt%). The solution was evaporated at 80 °C until a viscous gel formed. Then, it was dried into dry gel at 120 °C. The dry gel was ignited in air and burned into dendritic powders. Finally, the precursor powder was sintered at 1200 °C for 3 h.

First, Sr(NO3)2 and Fe(NO3)3·9H2O with Sr:Fe atomic ratio of 1:12 were dissolved in deionized water by gentle heating. Then, the aqueous mixture was slowly poured into (NH4)2C2O4 · H2O solution and stirred for several minutes using a magnetic stirrer. The gelatinous precipitate was filtered and washed several times using deionized water until the pH value of the solution became neutral. The dried powders were sintered at 500 °C for 8 h in air, and then sintered at 1100 °C for 8 h in air. Synthesis_Procedure: The glass of the initial composition SrFe8Cr4O19 –12Sr2B2O5 was prepared by rapid melt quenching. For that purpose, the stochiometric mixture of the starting reagents (SrCO3, Fe2O3, H3BO3, and Cr2O3, high purity grade, Aldrich, Saint Louis, MO, USA) was homogenized into a 10 g batch and fired at 900 °C for 2 h; then, the batch was ground and melted in a platinum crucible at 1350 °C. After a 1 h exposure, the melt was quenched between two rotating steel rollers to form glassy flakes. The glass ceramics were formed by isothermal heat treatment of the glass at annealing temperatures (Tann) of 600–900 °C during 2 h. Then, the samples were treated with 3% hydrochloric acid to dissolve the borate matrix and to leach the magnetic particles, which were separated from the solution by centrifugation, thoroughly washed with distilled water, and dried.

In this experiment, Sr1-xTbxFe12-yCoyO19 (x = 0.04 mol; y = 0.0, 0.10, 0.20, 0.30, 0.40, 0.50 mol) ferrite was prepared by ceramic sintering. The process of the reaction to produce metal oxides is shown in Fig. 1. Raw materials required for the experiment: iron oxide powder (Mackin, 99%), strontium carbonate powder (Mackin, 99.9%), terbium pentoxide powder (Chinese rare earths, 99.99%), cobalt oxide powder (Mackin, 99.9%), the raw materials to be weighed are calculated according to the proportion of molar percentage. The raw material is put into the ball mill for ball grinding, the speed is set at 550 r/min, and the ball grinding time is 4 h. The mixture after ball milling is poured into the beaker to settle, and the sediment is put into the drying box for drying. The temperature of the drying box is set at 150 °C and the drying time is 5 h. The dried mixture was ground and sieved, and the ground powder was put into the Muffle furnace for high temperature pre-burning, the processing temperature was 1180 °C, the pre-burning time was set to 3 h, and finally the strontium ferrite powder sample was obtained. The powder sample is put into the ball mill for secondary ball milling. The purpose of secondary ball milling is to make the strontium ferrite powder more uniform, which is convenient for subsequent compaction treatment. The strontium ferrite powder was divided into two parts, and one part was used to test the properties of the powder. Another strontium ferrite powder was pressed. The pressed block ferrite was put into the Muffle furnace for high temperature sintering, the sintering temperature was set at 1200 °C, and the sintering time was 3 h. Finally, the block M-type strontium ferrite was obtained, and the block ferrite was polished and polished on the surface to reduce the error of the subsequent magnetic properties test. The preparation process is shown in Fig. 2.

Sb-doped strontium hexaferrite powders, SrFe12-xSbxO19 (x = 0.00, 0.02, 0.04, 0.06, 0.08), were synthesized via a sol-gel auto-combustion route. Analytical grade precursors viz., strontium nitrate [Sr(NO3)2], ferric nitrate nano-hydrate [Fe(NO3)3⋅9H2O] citric acid monohydrate and ethylene glycol were used. Stoichiometric amounts of Sr(NO3)2 and Fe(NO3)3⋅9H2O were dissolved separately in 30 mL and 50 mL of deionized water respectively. The resulting solutions were then mixed under continuous stirring. Citric acid monohydrate was then introduced into the solution maintaining the metal ion to citric acid ratio at 1:1.5 to ensure effective chelation and prevent undesirable precipitation of metal ions. The mixed solution was maintained at 80 °C under continuous stirring at 400 rpm in a magnetic hot plate for 2 h. For Sb doping, the appropriate amount of Sb2O3 was dispersed in 1.5 mL of concentrated nitric acid and 2 mL of deionized water, followed by heating for 20 min and ultrasonication for 30 min to ensure dissolution. The cooled Sb solution was added dropwise to the metal–citric acid solution under constant magnetic stirring. Ethylene glycol was then added in a 1:1 M ratio with citric acid to facilitate gel formation and promote thorough mixing. As the gel became increasingly viscous, the stirrer was removed. The temperature was gradually increased to ~150 °C, and the gel was then transferred to a heating mantle for uniform heating and to initiate auto-combustion, yielding a voluminous and porous precursor powder. The resulting ash residue was ground and calcined at 900 °C for 4 h to obtain phase purity. The calcined powder obtained was then mixed with 2 wt% polyvinyl alcohol (PVA) as a binder and thoroughly ground to ensure uniform mixing. The powder was then uniaxially pressed into circular pellets of 8 mm diameter under an applied pressure of approximately 100 kg/cm2 using a hydraulic press. The pellets were sintered at 1100 °C for 3 h to achieve sufficient densification and enhance mechanical strength.

Synthesis_Procedure: The pure phase hexagonal ferrite, BaFe12-xSmxO19 with (x = 0.0, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 1.0) is prepared using a low cost citrate precursor sol–gel method. Chemicals used in this synthesis process were of high purity grade namely, Ba (NO3)2, Fe(NO3)3 and Sm (NO3)2 (Alfa Aesar, 99.9% purity). Citric acid worked as fuel during synthesis. The stoichiometric ratio of citric acid to metal cations was maintained to be 1:3 during solution preparation. At first, we weigh calculated proportion of chemical nitrates and dissolve it into individual beakers containing minimal amount of deionized water. Followed by pouring of these individual solutions into a single beaker and shifting the pH of this solution to 7 using drop wise addition of ammonia. Then this solution is kept on hot plate magnetic stirrer at temperature of 120℃ under continuous stirring, till a viscous like material is visible. In next step, this viscous jelly like substance is transferred into a hot air oven set at temperature 250℃ for 1 h for self-propagating combustion reaction to occur. As such we get a fluffy like ash powder, which is crushed down to fine powders using mortar and pestle. The powdered samples were then put into a microprocessor based annealing furnace, in alumina crucibles separately at 850℃ for 2 h each, with a heating rate of 4℃/ min.

The non-magnetic element zinc (d10 configuration) doped barium hexaferrite (BaFe12-xZnxO19, x = 0.0, 0.2, 0.4 and 0.6) have been synthesized by following modified citric acid based sol-gel method, because it is cost-effective [11]. The M-type SrCaLa hexaferrites with chemical compositions of Sr0.5Ca0.2La0.3Fe12.0−2x(SnMg)xO19 (0.0 ≤ x ≤ 0.5) were synthesized by ball milling and calcining. The starting materials used in this study were SrCO3 (99% purity), CaCO3 (99% purity), La2O3 (99% purity), Fe2O3 (99% purity), SnO2 (99% purity) and MgO (99% purity). They were used as such without further treatment. The starting powders were weighted in accordance with the ratios of the chemical composition. A ball mill was used with a ball to powder of 10:1. The milling was carried out for 9 h with a rotate speed of 80 rpm. After milling, the mixed powders were dried in a drying oven in the air, and then calcined in a muffle furnace at 1250 °C for 2.0 h in air. Next, the calcined samples were shattered to particles less than 50 lm by a vibration mill. In order to relieve the stress, the shattered particles were annealed in a muffle furnace at 780 °C for 1.5 h.

Synthesis_Procedure: BaM doped with Zn2+-Zr4+ was synthesized via sol-gel auto combustion methods using metal nitrate to fuel (citric acid) ratio of 1:1.5. Analytical grade chemicals such as ferric nitrate, Barium nitrate, zinc nitrate, zirconyl nitrate and citric acid were used without further purification. Metal salts were dissolved in double distilled water in stoichiometric ratio separately and then citric acid was added at ambient temperature with constant magnetic stirring. Ammonia was added drop wise to adjusted pH 7. The resultant solution was heated at 80-100°C for 3-4 hours with continuous magnetic stirring. With continuous heating excessive water evaporates and honey like highly viscous brown gel was formed. This gel was put in oven at 200-250°C for 1-2 hour after which auto combustion occurs resulting in a precursor powder material. The precursor material was grounded with motor pastel into fine powder form. Further this powder was calcined at 900°C for 6 hours in muffle furnace to remove impurities and half-baked M-Type BAM amorphous phase into single domain crystalline phase.

Metal salts were dissolved in double distilled water in stoichiometric ratio separately and then citric acid was added at ambient temperature with constant magnetic stirring. Ammonia was added drop wise to adjusted pH 7. The resultant solution was heated at 80-100°C for 3-4 hours with continuous magnetic stirring. With continuous heating excessive water evaporates and honey like highly viscous brown gel was formed. This gel was put in oven at 200-250°C for 1-2 hour after which auto combustion occurs resulting in a precursor powder material. The precursor material was grounded with motor pastel into fine powder form. Further this powder was calcined at 900°C for 6 hours in muffle furnace to remove impurities and half-baked M-Type BAM amorphous phase into single domain crystalline phase.

M-type hexaferrite samples have been synthesized by the conventional ceramic techniques. Compositions were chosen to according to the chemical composition Ca0.6Sr0.1La0.3Fe12 − xAlxO19, where Al content (x) varied from 0 to 1.4 with about 0.2 increment. All the starting materials used (CaCO3, SrCO3, La2O3, Fe2O3 and Al 2O3) were powders of analytical grade. Firstly, mixed powders of the precursor materials prepared by the wet-mixing method were calcined in a muffle furnace at 1260 °C for 2.0 h in the air. The calcined samples were shattered to particles less than 100 mm using a vibration mill, and then annealed in a muffle furnace at 750 °C for 1.0 h in order to relieve the stress.

Synthesis_Procedure: Desired metal nitrates in appropriate ratios were taken in the minimum amount of distilled water followed by the addition of citric acid (citric acid to total metal ions =1:1) and stirred until a homogenous mixture was obtained. The molar ratio of strontium was kept higher, i.e. 1.2, to maintain the stoichiometry of the product in these samples because of higher solubility of Sr(NO3)2 as compared to Fe(NO3)3.9H2O. The total weight of starting materials was 20 g. The pH was settled at 7 by the addition of NH4OH (35%) solution drop by drop using vigorous stirring at 70 °C. Dehydration of the solution was then carried out on a hotplate at 80 °C until a brown gel was formed. Dry gels prepared were heated in air at 220 °C to invoke ignition. Upon ignition,a large amount of gases were liberated and a light weight voluminous powder was formed quickly (Fig. 1). The material was finely ground and calcinated at 1100 °C for 5 h in a muffle furnace where the heating rates were maintained at 5 °C/min. The material was allowed to naturally cool and compressed at 8 t to make pellets of 10 mm diameter and of 2 mm thickness.

The hexaferrite samples of stoichiometric formula Sr0.54Ca0.46AlxFe12-xO19 (SCAFO - x) with Al doping concentration x = 2.0, 4.0, 5.5 and 6.5 were prepared by a standard solid-state reaction method which involves the reaction of Strontium Carbonate (SrCO3), Calcium Carbonate (CaCO3), Iron oxide (Fe2O3) and Aluminum oxide (Al2O3) in appropriate molecular ratios according to the reaction as follows: 54SrCO3 + 46CaCO3 + (1-x)Fe2O3 + xAl2O3 → Sr0.54Ca0.46AlxFe12-xO19 + CO2 (1) A schematic representation of the hexaferrite synthesis process is shown in Fig. 1(a). High purity powders of SrCO3, CaCO3, Fe2O3, and Al2O3 (Sigma-Aldrich, 99.9% purity) were weighed according to their stoichiometric ratios, thoroughly mixed and ground for 12 h in an agate mortar using isopropyl alcohol as a wet grinding medium to ensure a homogeneous compound mixture. The resulting powder, corresponding to different hexaferrite compositions, was then calcined at an optimized temperature of 1350 °C for 24 h (Fig. 1(b)). To achieve uniformity, the calcined powders were reground in a mortar and pestle for 2–3 h with a small amount of binder (3% polyvinyl alcohol aqueous solution). The obtained powders were subsequently pressed uniaxially under a pressure of 3000 psi using a stainless-steel die punch, forming pellets with approximate dimensions of 10 mm in diameter and 3 mm in thickness. These pellets were then sintered at a temperature of 1400 °C for 6 h, following a controlled heating and cooling rate of 5 °C/min in a programmable muffle furnace.

Strontium nitrate (Sr(NO3)2, ACS reagent, 99.0% purity), iron(III) nitrate nonahydrate (Fe(NO3)3⋅9H2O, ACS reagent, 98.0% purity), aluminium nitrate nonahydrate (Al(NO3)3.9H2O, ACS reagent, 98.0% purity), calcium nitrate (Ca(NO3)2, ACS reagent, 97.0% purity), Manganese nitrate tetrahydrate (Mn(NO3)2.4H2O, ACS reagent, 98.0% purity) as inorganic reactants were used as the initial salt for the synthesis of pure and cation substituted SFO. All the chemicals were purchased from Alfa Aesar. Citric acid (C6H8O7) was used as chelating agent, Ammonium Hydroxide (NH4OH) (Make: Merck) was used as pH adjuster, and deionized water as the solvent. The starting precursors were all of analytical purity and used without further purification. Sr0.8Ca0.2Fe10Al2-yMnyO19 (0 ≤ y ≤ 2) has been synthesized using the SGAC method with Fe/Sr molar ratio of 9.23:1, as schematically illustrated in Fig. 2. The inorganic salts (Sr(NO3)2, (Fe(NO3)3.9H2O), (Al (NO3)3.9H2O), Ca(NO3)2, and Mn(NO3)2.4H2O were dissolved in deionized water and stirred on a hotplate at 70 °C. After a clear solution was obtained, C6H8O7 was added to the above solution (citric acid to total metal ions molar ratio of 1:1), and subsequently stirred on hot plate at 90 °C. Afterward, the pH of the resulting mixture was adjusted to 7 by dropwise addition of NH4OH using a pipette. Subsequently, the final solution was continuously stirred for several hours at 90 °C until a highly viscous wet gel was formed. The obtained gel was then allowed to ignite in air through the auto-combustion reaction. As a result of this reaction, an as-burnt product with a voluminous and treelike structure was obtained. Then the obtained products were collected and crushed using an agate mortar pastel. The as-prepared powders were calcined in a muffle furnace at 950 °C for 1 h at a heating rate of 10 °C/min in air ambient.
Journal: Journal of Magnetism and Magnetic Materials

Synthesis_Procedure: This study reports the fabrication of hexagonal ferrite ceramics with the nominal composition BaFe11.5CuxZn0.25-xSn0.25O19 (x = 0.05, 0.10, 0.15, 0.20) via a conventional solid-state reaction sintering route. Highpurity BaCO3 (99.0%, Sinopharm Chemical Reagent Co., Ltd., lot No. 20250530), Fe2O3 (99%, reagent grade, Shanghai Macklin Biochemical Technology Co., Ltd., lot No. C17524742), CuO (≥99.0%, analytical grade, Sinopharm Chemical Reagent Co., Ltd., lot No. 20250312), ZnO (≥99.0%, pharmaceutical test grade, Sinopharm Chemical Reagent Co., Ltd., lot No. 20250113), and SnO2 (≥99.95%, metals basis, Aladdin Industrial Corporation, lot No. E2528656) powders were weighed according to the stoichiometric ratios and subjected to planetary ball milling at 250 rpm for 12 h in ethanol to ensure homogeneous mixing. The resultant slurry was dried at 60 °C, manually ground, and calcined at 1000 °Cfor 3 h in a muffle furnace. The calcined powder was then milled again for 12 h to improve particle size uniformity. After drying, the powder was uniaxially pressed into cylindrical pellets (diameter: 1.27 cm) under 8 MPa in a hot press furnace. Hot pressing was conducted using a SiC mold (outer diameter: 4 cm) lined with a ceramic tube (inner diameter: 1.27 cm) to facilitate demolding. The inner walls and bottom of the mold were coated with boron nitride (BN) spray to prevent adhesion. For comparison, selected pellets were pressureless sintered in a muffle furnace at 1100 °C. The remaining samples were densified via hot pressing: the temperature was first increased to 800 °C under ambient pressure in air, at which point a uniaxial pressure of 8 MPa was applied. The system was then heated to 975 °C and held for 85 min under constant pressure, followed by natural cooling to room temperature under atmospheric conditions.

We synthesized polycrystalline BaFe8Al2Zn2O19 hexaferrite using a sol-gel auto-combustion method. We dissolved analytical-grade barium, iron, aluminum, and zinc nitrates in deionized water according to the stoichiometry of the above-mentioned composition. Citric acid was added as a chelating agent and fuel for combustion. The pH of the solution was carefully maintained at approximately 7 by slowly adding aqueous ammonia [33]. The mixture was heated to approximately 85 °C while being stirred with a magnet until it formed a thick gel. Subsequently, heat treatment caused self-ignition at approximately 250 °C, resulting in a fine, ash-like powder. First, the burned powder was carefully ground to ensure that the particles were evenly spread out. Then, it was pre-calcined in air at 900 °C for 4 h to remove any organic material and initiate the crystallization process. Subsequently, the powder was pressed into pellets (≈5 mm radius, ≈2 mm thickness) at a pressure of 300 MPa. Sintering in ambient air was performed at 1200, 1225, 1250, 1275, and 1300 °C for 4 h. The sintering temperature range of 1200–1300 °C was selected based on prior literature on Al/Znsubstituted BaM hexaferrites, which indicates phase formation and optimal densification occur within this window, and was further supported by preliminary experiments assessing phase purity and microstructural evolution. The temperature was increased and decreased at a rate of 5 °C/min to prevent the grains from growing too large [34]. Fig. 1 shows a schematic overview of the entire synthesis process.

Using the Citrate auto-combustion method, the following nano samples were produced: SrFe12O19, SrFe11.5Co0.5O19, Sr0.95Dy0.05Fe12O19, and Sr0.95Dy0.05Fe11.5Co0.5O19. Citric acid (C6H8O7), cobalt nitrate Co(NO3)2, Dysprosium nitrate Dy(NO3)3·6H2O, and iron nitrate Fe(NO3)3.(H2O)9 were the raw materials. The starting concentrations of the precursors for Sr0.95Dy0.05Fe11.5Co0.5O19, such as the Strontium (2.010485g), cobalt (1.4552g), Dysprosium (0.219295g), and iron (46.46g) nitrates, matched the specific ferrites' stoichiometric ratios. These precursors were combined with citric acid (24.9769g) in a powder phase, and the mixture was then vigorously stirred while judicious drops from water that were distilled were added to get the dissolved mixture. Subsequently, the pH of the mixture was brought to 7.0. The mixture was heated to 250 C to start the process of breaking down citric acid, this powder was then ground as well as burned at 1000 °C, over 6 h to reach the required phase. All other samples [SrFe12O19, SrFe11.5Co0.5O19, and Sr0.95Dy0.05Fe12O19,] were prepared with the same sequence as mentioned above.

The entire explored poly-crystalline sintered Sr1-xCexFe12-xCoxO19 (0≤x≤0.25/x=0.05) nano hexaferrites (SCFCO-N-Hs) were synthesized by mixing of highly graded pure Fe2O3 (98%), SrCO3 (99%), Ce2O3 (99%), and CoO (99%) powders under the conventional solid-state reaction approach. Figure 1 shows the synthesization steps of the process. Primarily, the entire preparatory materials were heterogeneous in an indented stoichiometric ratio of 1:12. Then the blend of these rare compounds was refined in distilled water and milled at an angular frequency of 300 rpm for 2 hours in a planetary ball milling mechanism (Pulverisette; Fritsch GmbH, Germany), with hardened steel balls of diameter 8 mm, 10 mm, and 12 mm. The ball to powder ratio elected as 10:1 and the ball-to-ball ratio was 1:1.5:2. The extracted wet powder mixture then filtered, dried, and crushed. The execration of SCFCO-N-Hs powders is as follows, (1-x)SrCO3 + ((12−x)/2)Fe2O3 + xCoO + (x/2)Ce2O3 → SrxCexFe12−xCoxO19 + CO2 ↑ These dried powder samples then sintered in a box coke oven for 2 hours at 1260 C0. After that, the calcite samples milled into powder of particles sizes less than 100 nm in a vibrating mill.

The precursor solution can be expressed as (Co2+ /Zn2+ /Ca2+ ):Sm3+ :Sr2+ :Fe3+ = (x/y/z):0.2:(1 ‒ z): [11.80 ‒ (x/y)] (x/y/z = 0, 0.05, 0.10, 0.15, and 0.20) (all ratios are molar ratios). The precursor solutions were ultrasonically stirred for 1 h to obtain a homogeneous solution. The concentration of Fe3+ in the solution was maintained at 0.20 mol/L. The exact molar quantities of all reagents used in the precursor solution preparation are summarized in Table S1. The chemical reagents used in this study were of analytical grade and obtained from Sinopharm Chemical Reagent Co., Ltd., Macklin, and Aladdin. Specifically, iron(III) nitrate nonahydrate (Fe(NO3)3⋅9H2O, AR) and strontium nitrate (Sr(NO3)2 , AR) were purchased from Sinopharm Chemical Reagent Co., Ltd. Samarium(III) nitrate hexahydrate (Sm(NO3)3⋅6H2O, 99.9%) was supplied by Macklin. Cobalt(II) nitrate hexahydrate (Co(NO3)3⋅6H2O, 99%) was obtained from Aladdin, while zinc(II) nitrate hexahydrate (Zn(NO3)2⋅6H2O, 99.0%) and calcium nitrate tetrahydrate (Ca(NO3)2⋅4H2O, 98.5%) were sourced from Sinopharm Chemical Reagent Co., Ltd. All reagents were used without further purification. The Sm‒(Co2+ /Zn2+ /Ca2+ ) co-doped SrFe12O19 powders were synthesized via ultrasonic spray pyrolysis. The precursor solution was nebulized using an ultrasonic atomizer and transported into a tube furnace with three temperature zones set at 300°C, 600°C, and 1180°C, where the solvent evaporated, and the solid precursor decomposed and sintered into fine spherical powders.

Synthesis_Procedure: The SrFe10−xNixAl2O19 (0 ≤ x ≤ 0.3) hexaferrite powders were prepared by using sol–gel auto-combustion method. High-purity chemicals including strontium nitrate Sr(NO3)2·4H2O (Sigma–Aldrich, ≥99%), iron nitrate Fe(NO3)3·9H2O (Sigma– Aldrich, ≥98%), nickel nitrate Ni(NO3)2·6H2O (LobaChemie, ≥98%), and aluminum nitrate Al(NO3)3·9H2O (Sigma–Aldrich, ≥98%) were individually dissolved in distilled water. Then the solutions were combined in a single beaker and stirred magnetically until obtaining a homogeneous solution. Citric acid (Sigma–Aldrich, ≥ 99.5%) was added in a 1:2 ratio to the solution, followed by neutralization with ammonia. After approximately 3 h of stirring at 80 °C on a hot plate, a viscous liquid gel was formed. Subsequently, upon further temperature increase, the gel underwent a self-combustion process, transforming into powder form. The resulting powders were ground at room temperature for 1 h using an agate mortar and subsequently calcined at 1200 °C (Ref. 14) for 3 h with a heating rate of 3 °C/min.

The schematic of the synthesis process was illustrated in Fig. 1. The reagents used in the experiment were listed in Table 1. A certain amount of Sr(NO)2 and Fe(NO3)3·9H2O were dissolved in 50 ml of deionized water. Then citric acid was added to the above mixture (weighed by a molar ratio of citric acid to metal ions of 1:1) and stirred well, adjusting the pH to 7 and the water bath temperature to 70 °C. Subsequently, the solution was heated and stirred in a constanttemperature magnetic agitator until it became soluble, and then dried at 250 °C for 3 h to obtain the gel [31]. The gel was ground into a fine powder and calcined at 800 °C, 900 °C, 1000 °C, and 1100 °C for 3 h in a chamber resistance furnace. The samples were recorded as SFO-800, SFO-900, SFO1000, and SFO-1100, respectively. The Sr1 − xPrxFe12O19 (0 ≤ x ≤ 0.1) and Sr0.95Re0.05Fe12O19 (Re = La, Pr, Nd, Dy, Yb) samples followed the same procedure with a calcination temperature of 900 °C. The Sr1 − xPrxFe12O19 samples were recorded as SPFO-0, SPFO-0.025, SPFO-0.05, SPFO-0.075 and SPFO-0.1 with x = 0, 0.025, 0.05, 0.075 and 0.1, respectively. The Sr0.95Re0.05Fe12O19 samples were recorded as SLFO-0.05, SPFO-0.05, SNFO-0.05, SDFO-0.05, SYFO0.05, with Re = La, Pr, Nd, Dy, and Yb, respectively.

Synthesis_Procedure: The sol-gel auto-combustion method was adopted as the synthesis technique for the present work. Strontium nitrate [Sr(NO3)2], ferric nitrate [Fe(NO3)3·9H2O], aluminum nitrate [Al(NO3)3·9H2O], nickel nitrate [Ni(NO3)2.6H2O], cobalt nitrate [Co(NO3)2·6H2O], and glycine (C2H5NO2) of AR grade were used and metal nitrate versus fuel ratio was taken as 1:1. The number of moles taken for each compound is represented through the reaction given below (where x = 0.1, 0.2): [1 − x]Sr(NO3)2 + [10]Fe(NO3)3·9H2O + [2]Al(NO3)3·9H2O + [x][Ni(NO3)2·6H2O/Co(NO3)2·6H2O] + C2H5NO2 + NH4OH → [Sr1−xNixAl2Fe10O19/Sr1−xCoxAl2Fe10O19] + NH3 ↑ + CO2 ↑ + NOχ ↑ + H2O ↑ (1) The stoichiometry amount of each metal nitrate was dissolved in the di-ionized water and stirred for 30 min. Later, all the metal nitrate solutions were mixed, and the glycine solution was added to it; then the solution was given heat, and it was kept at 80 °C for 30 min. To neutralize the solution (pH = 7), the ammonia solution (NH4OH) was added to it. Then continuous heat was provided to the solution until it changed into a gel form, and the constant supply of heat resulted in a self-auto-combustion reaction. Then the burnt powder was ground using agate and mortar and was sintered at 1100 °C for 4 h. Afterwards, the final compound was used for various characterizations (Fig. 1). For the dielectric studies, pellets of diameter of 1 cm and thickness of 2 mm were prepared.

M-type Sr hexaferrite (Sr1–xLaxFe12O19; x = 0.00, 0.03, 0.06, 0.09, 0.12, and 0.15) was prepared by a conventional solidphase method. Iron oxide (Fe2O3; 99.7%), strontium carbonate (SrCO3; 99%), and lanthanum oxide (La2O3; 98%) were used as starting materials without any treatment. We weighed six groups of drugs according to different molar ratios, put the weighed samples into a nylon tank, and mixed the balls, materials, and water at a ratio of 10:1:1.1. We next used a planetary ball mill for wet grinding and mixing. The ball milling time was 5 h. The homogenized slurry was dried and pressed into a muffle furnace for sintering at a heating rate of 5 °C/min up to 1240 °C, held for 2 h, and then cooled via furnace cooling. Next, we removed the sintered sample, which was crushed, ground, and tested.

Synthesis_Procedure: The ultrasonic irradiation-assisted sonochemical method was employed to produce the pure phases of Sr0.8Ca0.2AlxCoxFe12−2xO19 hexaferrite. (C2H3O2)2 Sr, (C2H3O2)2 Fe, (CH3 COO)2 Co, (C2H3O2)3 Al, and (CH3CO2)2 Ca (with their stoichiometric weight proportions ofSr:Ca:Al:Co:Fe = 0.8:0.2:x:x:12-2x) were diluted in 150 ml of di-ionized (DI) water and in diethylene glycol (C4H10O3). The entire solution was exposed to high-intensity ultrasonic irradiation (20 kHz frequency and 70 W power) for 120 min. The temperature of the solution was 90 °C during the ultrasonication because of the very high number of collisions. The synthesized product was washed several times with DI water. The Sr0.8Ca0.2AlxCoxFe12−2xO19 powder was dried at 100 °C for 12 h, and then sintered at 1000 °C for 4 h in air atmosphere.

Synthesis_Procedure: Ba0.54Ca0.46Fe12− x AlxO19 (x = 2.3, 2.4 and 2.5) powders were synthesized via sol-gel auto-combustion method. Aluminium nitrate Al (NO3)3.6H2O (Sigma Aldrich, ≥98%), Iron nitrates Fe(NO3)3.9H2O (Sigma Aldrich, ≥98%), Calcium nitrates Ca(NO3)2.4H2O (Sigma Aldrich, ≥99%) and Barium nitrates Ba(NO3)2 (Sigma Aldrich, ≥99%), were dissolved separately in distilled water, then the solutions of Iron, aluminium, calcium and barium nitrates were mixed in a larger beaker under continuous stirring. Subsequently, an aqueous solution of citric acid C6H8O7 was introduced into the metal-nitrate solution, maintaining a molar ratio of metal ions to citric acid of 1:1, then a solution of Ammonia hydroxide was added to the solution to maintain the pH at 7. The solution was heated at 80 °C until obtaining a gel, the gel was after that heated at 200 °C until it is spontaneously burned and turned into a voluminous porous powder. The obtained gel was crushed and annealed in air at 1250 °C for 3 h, with a heating rate of 3 °C per minute.

Synthesis_Procedure: In this study, Sr1-xNdxAlyFe12-yO19 (0.00 ≤ x ≤ 0.20, 0.00 ≤ y ≤ 2.00) is produced with Al3+ and Nd3+ dopant using the auto-combustion solgel process, as illustrated in Fig. 2. The Ba0.5Sr0.5DyxFe12-xO19 (0.00 ≤ x ≤ 0.15) samples were prepared via the sol-gel auto-combustion technique, which is well-suited for obtaining homogeneous and fine-grained hexaferrite powders. The Analytical-grade Ba(NO3)2, Sr(NO3)2, Fe(NO3)3⋅9H2O, and Dy (NO3)3⋅xH2O (≥99.9% purity, Sigma-Aldrich) were used as precursor salts without further purification. In a typical synthesis procedure, stoichiometric amount of Barium nitrate [Ba(NO3)2], Strontium nitrate [Sr(NO3)2], Ferric nitrate nonahydrate [Fe(NO3)3⋅9H2O], and Dysprosium nitrate [Dy(NO3)3⋅xH2O] were accurately weighed and dissolved in DI water under continuous magnetic stirring to form a clear and uniform aqueous solution. Citric acid was employed as a chelating and fuel agent and it was added to the solution in a molar ratio of 3:1 relative to the total metal cations for the combustion process. The resulting mixture was then gently heated to approximately 80 °C with constant stirring until it transformed into a viscous gel, indicating successful complexation between the metal ions and citric acid. To facilitate proper gelation and maintain a near-neutral pH, ammonia solution was introduced gradually in a dropwise manner until the pH reached around 7. Once the gel was formed, it was subjected to further heating, leading to spontaneous ignition and combustion. This exothermic reaction produced a voluminous, fluffy precursor powder. The precursor was finely milled with an agate mortar and pestle to achieve homogeneous particle size prior to calcination. Calcination was performed in a muffle furnace at 1100 °C for 5 h, resulting in phase-pure hexaferrite powders ready for further structural and magnetic analyses.

The BaFe12-xMnxO19 (x = 0.0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4) powders were prepared by hydrothermal synthesis. The precursor was a mixture of an aqueous solution of iron nitrate nonahydrate Fe(NO3)3⋅9H2O, barium nitrate Ba(NO3)2 and manganese chloride MnCl2⋅4H2O with an aqueous solution of sodium hydroxide NaOH in proportion 60 ml/20 ml, respectively. The solutions were prepared with the expectation that in the final volume (80 mL) the concentration of iron ions would be 0.25 M, the (Fe3++Mn2+)/Ba2+ ratio would be 9, and the OH/NO3 ratio would be 2.5. After that, the resulting mixture was placed in a 100 ml Teflon vessel, hermetically sealed and placed in an oven. The autoclave was slowly heated to 180 oC over 2 h and maintained at this temperature for 4 h. The resulting precipitate and liquid solution were separated using a centrifuge. The precipitate was washed and dried at 90 °C for 8 h. The dry residue was ground in an agate mortar and annealed in a muffle furnace in air. The heating rate was 15° /min, the final temperature was 900 °C, and the annealing time was 1 h. To remove possible side phases, the samples were washed in hydrochloric acid HCl (10%) and distilled water and then sent back to the drying oven for 8 h at a temperature of 90 °C.

SrFe12-xAlxO19 (x = 0, 1, 1.4, 2, 2.4) were prepared by sol–gel combustion from Fe(NO3)3⋅9H2O, Al(NO3)3⋅9H2O, and Sr(NO3)2 as metal precursors. The molar ratio of total trivalent cations to strontium was fixed at (Fe3++Al3+)/Sr2+ = 11. This value, slightly lower than the stoichiometric ratio of 12 for SrFe12O19, was chosen to introduce a small excess of Sr2+ in the reaction mixture to compensate for possible Sr volatilization during the combustion and calcination steps and to favor single-phase formation. After gelation (citric acid, pH=7), the dried gel was combusted at 300 °C, ground, and annealed at 1100 °C for 6 h in air. This series is referred to as SFAO_x and SFO, respectively. More info on the synthesis is reported in Ref [24].

Rare earth-substituted strontium hexaferrite samples (Sr1-xRExFe12O19) were synthesized using the Pechini sol-gel method, targeting substitution levels of x = 0.01, 0.025, 0.050, 0.075, and 0.10. Additionally, unsubstituted strontium hexaferrite (x = 0.0) was prepared to use as a reference. The synthesis was carried out using chemical reagents and solvents such as strontium nitrate (Sr(NO3)2, Meyer, 99%), iron nitrate nonahydrate (Fe(NO3)3•9H2O, Sigma Aldrich, 98%), citric acid (C6H8O7, Sigma Aldrich, 99.5%), and ethylene glycol (C2H6O2, Sigma Aldrich, 99.8%). Depending on the substitution series, one of the following rare earth nitrates was incorporated: gadolinium nitrate hexahydrate (Gd(NO3)3•6H2O, Sigma Aldrich, 99.9%), samarium nitrate hexahydrate (Sm(NO3)3•6H2O, Sigma Aldrich, 99.9%), neodymium nitrate hexahydrate (Nd(NO3)3•6H2O, Sigma Aldrich, 99.9%), praseodymium nitrate hexahydrate (Pr(NO3)3•6H2O, Sigma Aldrich, 99.9%), or lanthanum nitrate hexahydrate (La(NO3)3•6H2O, Fluka, 99%). The formation of substituted hexaferrites followed the reaction scheme shown in Eq. (1). (1 − x) Sr(NO3)2 + (x)RE(NO3)3 + 12 Fe(NO3)3 →Sr1− x RExFe12O19 + (38 + x)NO2 ↑ + (9.5 + 0.5x)O2 ↑ (1) The precursor salts were carefully weighed in stoichiometric proportions required to obtain 1.0 g of hexaferrite powder for each sample. Reagent quantities were calculated considering the targeted stoichiometry of the respective substituted hexaferrites. Moreover, a 3 wt% excess of rare earth nitrate was added to compensate for potential material loss during the sintering process [18]. The quantities of the rare earth precursors used for the synthesis of the corresponding hexaferrite samples are listed in Table 1. The synthesis process involved dissolving stoichiometric amounts of nitrate salts in 20 mL of deionized water under magnetic agitation. Subsequently, ethylene glycol and citric acid were added in a 4:1 M ratio, together with an additional 20 mL of deionized water. The mixture was first heated to 85 °C to remove excess water and subsequently raised to 100 °C to promote the polyesterification reaction. The resulting resin for each composition was subjected to thermal treatment at 380 °C for 40 min, followed by manual grinding in an agate mortar. Finally, the obtained powders were calcined in air at 1100 °C for 4 h and allowed to cool down gradually inside the furnace.

So we used citrate-nitrate gel combustion method to obtain aluminum-substituted barium hexaferrite BaAl4Fe8O19. Barium nitrate (Ba(NO3)2, analytical grade), aluminum nitrate nonahydrate (Al(NO3)3⋅9H2O, chemically pure), iron(III) nitrate nonahydrate (Fe(NO3)3⋅9H2O, pure), citric acid monohydrate (C6H8O7⋅H2O, pure), and 25 wt.% aqueous ammonia (NH4OH(aq), analytical grade) were used. This approach involved weighing nitrates in stoichiometric proportions. Citric acid was weighed at a rate of 3 moles of acid per 1 mol of total nitrates. The weighed portions were dissolved in a minimal amount of water, and the resulting solutions were mixed in a porcelain dish. After 15 min of room temperature stirring, the mixture was neutralized by adding an aqueous ammonia solution to a pH of 8 (monitored using universal indicator paper). The solution was then slowly evaporated in a boiling water bath until a honey-like mass was obtained. The resulting honey-like mass is presumably a mixture of barium, iron, and aluminum nitrates, ammonium citrate, and residual water. A porcelain cup containing the resulting mass was heated in a muffle furnace. During heating, final dehydration and thermal decomposition of the ammonium citrate and nitrates occur. Oxygen formed during the decomposition of the nitrates oxidizes the citric acid. Heating releases a large amount of gases, causing the mass to foam. Preliminary studies showed that heating should be done slowly, as rapid heating (over 1–2 h) causes the mass to swell excessively and may fall out of the cup. Therefore, the following heating program was used: 1) heating for 1 h to 100 °C; 2) holding for 2 h at 100 °C; 3) heating for 2 h to 150 °C; 4) holding for 2 h at 150 °C; 5) heating for 2 h to 200 °C; 6) holding for 2 h at 200 °C; cooling along with the furnace. This process resulted in the formation of a bulk xerogel. The xerogel was thoroughly ground and transferred to a porcelain crucible. To oxidize the residual carbon, the xerogel was heated in a muffle furnace at 500 °C for 6 h. The resulting material was ferritized in a corundum crucible. The method was firstly tested on pure barium hexaferrite. Ferritization temperature was selected as the variable parameter. X-ray phase analysis showed that holding the material at 900 °C for 4 h was sufficient for complete ferritization of BaFe12O19. Given that a higher sintering temperature is a priori required to obtain BaAl4Fe8O19, it was decided to ferritize it at 1100 °C for 4 h.

Synthesis_Procedure: The polycrystalline sample of BaFe11.6Mg0.05Mn0.05Ti0.2Ni0.1O19 was synthesized via the conventional solid-state reaction method, chosen for its robustness and reproducibility in producing phase-pure M-type hexaferrites with tailored microstructural features. The detailed sequence of the solid-state synthesis steps, including weighing, mixing, pre-calcination and final calcination, is summarized in the flow chart presented in Fig. 1. The starting materials BaCO3 (99.9%, Sigma-Aldrich), Fe2O3 (99.8%, Sigma-Aldrich), MgO (99.9%, Sigma-Aldrich), MnCO3 (99.5%, SigmaAldrich), Ni2O3 (99.9%, Sigma-Aldrich) and TiO2 (99.9%, Aldrich) were used as raw precursors were weighed in stoichiometric proportions according to the nominal reaction scheme: BaCO3 + 0.05MnCO3 + 0.05MgO + 0.05Ni2O3 + 0.2TiO2 + (6–0.2)Fe2O3 →BaFe11.6Mg0.05Mn0.05Ti0.2Ni0.1O19 + (1.005) CO2− 0.1O The mixed powders (~5 g per batch) were homogenized by manual grinding in an agate mortar using ethanol as a dispersing medium, then dried and pre-calcined at 700 °C for 24 h to decompose volatile components while preventing premature phase formation particularly relevant due to the low melting/decomposition points of BaCO3 and MgO. After regrinding, a final calcination at 1300 °C for 6 h in air was carried out to ensure full crystallization of the magnetoplumbite phase. Controlled heating and cooling rates (5 °C/min) minimized thermal stress and microcracking.

Synthesis_Procedure: All materials used were of analytical grade, including barium nitrate (Ba(NO3)2, Xilong, China, 99.5 %), ferric nitrate nonahydrate (Fe (NO3)3.9H2O, Keshi, China, 98.5 %), samarium(III) nitrate hexahydrate (Sm(NO3)3•6H2O, Macklin, China, 99.9 %), ammonia solution (NH3, Fuchen (Tianjin), China, 25–28 ωt.%), and citric acid (C6H8O7⋅H2O, Fuchen (Tianjin), China, 99.5 %). Sm doped barium hexaferrite structures were synthesized with chemical formula Ba1-xSmxFe12O19 (x = 0, 0.02, 0.05, 0.08, 0.10, 0.20) via sol–gel auto-combustion method. The flow chart was shown in Fig. 2. Ba(NO3)2, Fe(NO3)3•9H2O and Sm(NO3)3•6H2O were dissolved in deionized water under continuous stirring at room temperature. In this process, citric acid was utilized as a chelating agent with a molar ratio to metal cations at 2:1. After the solute is thoroughly stirred and dissolved, the ammonia solution was added dropwise into the prepared solution, adjusting the pH to approximately 7. The mixture was continuously stirred at room temperature to obtain homogenous solution. Then, the resulting mixture was placed into an oven and dried at 80 °C to evaporate water. The obtained viscous gel was subjected to a self-combustion reaction in an oven at 200 °C. The obtained powder was thoroughly ground and calcined in a muffle furnace at 1100 °C with a heating rate of 5 °C/min, which maintained for 5 h to obtain the final product.

Samples with the nominal composition BaAlxSmxFe12-xO19 (where x = 0.0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8) were synthesized using the sol-gel method. Microcrystalline samples of strontium M-type hexaferrite SrFe12-xInxO19 (with doping levels x = 1.7, 1.8 and 2.0 Indium atoms per formula unit (f.u.)) were synthesized via the citrate gel combustion method using nitrates Sr(NO3)2, Fe(NO3)3⋅9H2O, In(NO3)3⋅3H2O, (NH4)OH and C6H8O7 (all Sigma-Aldrich, technical grade, purity >98 %) as precursors. The as-synthesized powders were subsequently annealed at 1200 °C for 1 h in an air atmosphere. For nanoparticle production the SrFe12-xInxO19 microcrystalline powders were subjected to high-energy ball milling using a planetary ball mill PM 400 (Retsch, Germany) at a rotational speed of 400 rpm for 50 h. The milling medium comprised 1-octadecene with oleic acid (OA) added as a surfactant. A powder-to-ball mass ratio of 1:10 was maintained. Following milling, the particles were washed to remove residual 1-octadecene and transferred into dichloromethane (DCM). Ultrasonic homogenization was then performed to disrupt particle agglomerates. Subsequently, the particles were coated with hydrophilic biocompatible Pluronic F-127 copolymer to enable aqueous stabilization. For coating, powder suspensions were prepared in toluene. An aqueous solution of Pluronic F-127 was then introduced to the toluene suspensions. An emulsion was formed via ultrasonic homogenization. This emulsion was centrifuged, resulting in phase separation where the toluene migrated to form the upper phase. The toluene phase was carefully decanted and replaced with deionized water with subsequent sonication until a homogeneous sol is formed. After that the final hydrophilized nanoparticles were collected by centrifugation.

Ba-Zn hexaferrite nanoparticles were prepared by a sol-gel auto combustion process, which is an energy-saving process, requires low annealing temperatures to enhance crystal growth or particle size, and improves composition purity, also synthesizes ultrafine nano-sized particles with specific surface area, physicochemical properties, and fast reaction rate. The solutions (300 ml) contain stoichiometric quantities of Ba(NO3)2 .6H2O, Fe(NO3)2 .9H2O, and Zn(NO3)2 .6H2O. It was prepared by weighing the compositional atomic ratios and mixed under magnetic stirring for 30 min to get the precursor sol. For promoting the interaction of electronegative oxygen ions and electropositive ions, citric acid was selected as a chelating agent and also responsible for the binding of Zn2+ , Ba2+, and Fe3+ cations with anions (citrate 2− and citrate3− ), metal nitrate was surpassed during precipitation and water removal [32], [33]. Solution of citric acid (C6H8O7 .H2O) prepared in 300 ml of deionized water was dissolved into the mixture of nitrates under constant stirring. The molar ratio of metal ions to citric acid was kept 1:1. To get a pH of 7, a solution of ammonium hydroxide was added drop by drop to the resulting mixture, followed by a 5-hour heating process at 300 °C until the solvent completely evaporated. The remaining viscous gel of dark brown color was self-ignited and spread and swelled out of the container at the end. After the precursors are completely decomposed, a brown powder is formed. Finally, powder calcination is performed at 900o C for 7 hours. Using a mortar and pestle, a finely grind powder of Ba-Zn nanoparticles was obtained with a distinct phase [34], [35].

The process of synthesizing nano samples with specific chemical formulas using the flash auto-combustion technique as shown in Fig. 1. The samples produced include Sr(1-x) RExFe12O19 (where x = 0.05 and RE represents Sm and/or Dy). The methodology involves the careful combination of raw ingredients, thermal treatment, and grinding to achieve the desired phase of the materials. The raw materials used for the synthesis include Strontium Nitrate (Sr(NO3)2), Samarium Nitrate Hexahydrate (Sm(NO3)3·6H2O), Dysprosium Nitrate Hexahydrate (Dy(NO3)3·6H2O), Iron Nitrate, and Urea. These ingredients were combined in accordance with their stoichiometric ratios to ensure the correct chemical composition of the final products. A slight quantity of deionized water was added to the mixture of raw ingredients. The solution was then stirred at a temperature of 80 °C. This step was crucial for eliminating any fumes and ensuring the formation of a homogeneous powder. After stirring, the resultant solution was allowed to cool, resulting in the formation of a fine powder. This powder is the precursor for the subsequent sintering process. The produced powder was subjected to grinding to achieve a uniform particle size. Following this, the powder was sintered at a temperature of 1000 °C for a duration of 6 h. This thermal treatment is essential for achieving the necessary crystalline phase of the materials.

Crystalline Ba0.5Sr0.5Y1.0Fe11−xCox/2Alx/2O19 (x = 0.00, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 1.00) powders were prepared through the sol–gel auto-combustion route.35 Stoichiometric quantities of the respective metal nitrates were dissolved in approximately 200 mL of deionized water under constant stirring to obtain a transparent homogeneous solution. Citric acid was added as a chelating agent to promote uniform cation distribution. The pH of the mixed solution was carefully adjusted to around 8 by the slow addition of aqueous ammonia, facilitating gel formation. Continuous heating and stirring caused the solution to transform into a viscous gel, which subsequently underwent a spontaneous exothermic combustion reaction, yielding a voluminous and fluffy precursor powder. The as-burnt powders were calcined at 1200 °C for 6 h in a muffle furnace to achieve phase-pure, crystalline M-type hexaferrites with improved thermal stability.

The Ba0.5Sr0.5Fe12-2xLaxGdxO19 (x = 0, 0.05, 0.1, 0.15, and 0.2) particles were synthesized using metal nitrates such as Ba(NO3)2 (Sigma-Aldrich, ≥99 %), Sr (NO3)2 (Sigma-Aldrich, ≥99 %), Fe(NO3)3.9H2O (Sigma-Aldrich, ≥99 %), Gd (NO3)3.6H2O(Sigma-Aldrich, ≥99.9 %) and La (NO3)3.6H2O (Sigma-Aldrich, ≥99.9 %). Thereafter, the temperature of the plate was raised to approximately 200 °C until the combustion process took place. As a result, a brown powder was obtained and ground using an agate mortar and pestle. The powder was calcined for 2 h at 950 °C with a heating and cooling rate of 1 °C/min. All heat treatments were conducted in air.

In the experimentally synthesized La-Co codoped SFO samples through solid state reaction method, the doping concentration was controlled to maintain a La:Co ratio of 1:1, La (0.5 at%) and Co (0.56 at %) with total dopant content adjusted to approximately 1 mol% relative to the host cations. To ensure focus on experimentally relevant improvements, we synthesized only pristine and La-Co codoped SFO samples. La-only doping was excluded, as La, being non-magnetic, is known to degrade magnetic performance and has consistently shown reduced magnetization in previous studies [33–35] and also in our DFT results. The fabrication of La–Co codoped strontium hexaferrites was conducted through a traditional ceramic method. High-purity SrCO3 (97.5 %) and Fe2O3 (99 %) were meticulously weighed with exact stoichiometric ratios, in conjunction with La2O3 (98 %) and Co3O4 (98.5 %), to attain the specified doping levels. To ensure uniformity, the dry powders were thoroughly mixed before adding a 25 % polyvinyl alcohol (PVA) solution to aid in pellet formation. The concentration was selected to provide sufficient green compact strength and minimize drying cracks during pellet preparation. Although higher binder levels may promote porosity, the subsequent calcination at 1260 °C ensures complete removal of the organic phase, resulting in dense microstructures with well-developed grains. The mixture was then pressed into pellets and calcined at 1260 °C in a muffle furnace to achieve the desired magnetoplumbite phase. Following calcination, the pellets underwent crushing and grinding. To obtain fine and uniform particles, the powder was processed through wet ball milling in a rolling mill for a duration of 20 h.

A collection of Ba0.5Sr0.5Tb0.5Fe11.5-xPrxO19 (x = 0.00, 0.04, 0.08, 0.12) samples were prepared by utilizing the sol-gel self-propagating ignition technique. Despite any additional processing, the following raw materials were employed directly: Ba(NO3)2 (Merck; 99 %), Sr (NO3)2(99 %, Merck), citric acid (99.5 %, Sigma Aldrich), Tb (NO3)3⋅5H2O (Sigma Aldrich; 99.9 %,), Fe(NO3)3⋅9H2O (Merck; 99 %), Pr(NO3)3⋅6H2O (99 %, Macklin) and ammonia (25 %, Sigma Aldrich). First, a solution of metal salts was created by fully dissolving ferric, barium, strontium, praseodymium, and terbium nitrates in deionized water. Another solution is then created by adding citric acid to the solution after it has been uniformly combined with deionized water. Nitrates and citric acid have a molar ratio of 1:1. The pH of the solution was then adjusted to about 7 by adding ammonia water. To create a viscous liquid, the solution was then spun in an oil bath set at 90 °C. To create a dry gel, the viscous liquid was air-dried at 100 °C in an oven. To create a fluffy powder, heat processing was applied to the dried gel. The sample was then obtained by calcining the resulting powder for four hours at 1100 °C.

M-type hexaferrites with the chemical compositions Sr1−xLaxFe12−xMgxO19 (x = 0, 0.05, 0.1, 0.15) were synthesized via the conventional solid-state reaction method. The precursor and sintering additive powders—Fe2O3 (99.5%, industrial use), SiO2 (99.0%, industrial use), SrCO3, La2O3, MgO, CaO, CaCO3, Al2O3, Cr2O3, CuO (all 99.9% purity, Kojundo Chemical Lab. Co., Ltd., Sakado, Japan), and Bi2O3 (99.9% purity, Aldrich, St. Louis, MO, USA) —were weighed according to the desired cation ratios. Each powder mixture (50.00 g) was placed in a polypropylene bottle with yttria-stabilized ZrO2 balls and deionized (DI) water and ball-milled at a rotation speed of 100 rpm for 24 h. Then, the mixed powder was dried in an oven, placed in an alumina crucible, and calcined at a temperature of 1100 °C in air for 4 h. The calcined powders were ground, sieved, ballmilled again for 20 h, and dried. The ball-milled powders were pressed in a disk-shaped mold with a diameter of 30.0 mm at a pressure of approximately 15 MPa to produce green compact pellets. The pelletized samples were sintered in air at a temperature of 1230 °C for 2 h.

Synthesis_Procedure: The precursor materials used in this study were Barium Carbonate (BaCO3) powder with 99.5% purity and Iron (III) Oxide (Fe2O3) powder with a purity of over 99%, both obtained from SigmaAldrich. BaFe12O19 was synthesized using the solid-state reaction method. The precursor powders of BaCO3 and Fe2O3, as represented in the reaction equation (1), were then weighed according to stoichiometric calculations. BaCO3 + 6Fe2O3 → BaFe12O19 + CO2 (1) Next, the precursors were mixed using a mortar for 2 hours. Simultaneously, another batch of precursors was mixed using High Energy Milling (HEM). After mixing, the second sample was dried in an oven at 90°C for 12 hours. The samples were then sintered at 1200°C for 5 hours. After sintering, the samples were ground again using a mortar until fine and passed through a 200 mesh sieve. The samples were then ready for characterization.

Strontium chloride (SrCl2.6H2O), anhydrous Ferric chloride (FeCl3), Zinc nitrate Zn(NO3)2, diethylene glycol and sodium hydroxide were commercially purchased from Merck, India. Analytical grade chemicals were used without further purification all through the experiments. Zinc doped strontium ferrite metacomposites were synthesised by a facile route, schematically shown in Fig. 2. The processes are explained under this section. Hydrothermal method was used to prepare the samples. In this procedure, the nanostructured Sr1-xZnxFe12O19 (Sr and Fe ratio 1:8) with x fraction varying as 0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4 and 0.5 were prepared by dissolving appropriate amount of precursors like SrCl2.6H2O and anhydrous FeCl3 and Zn(NO3)2.6H2O were mixed with small amount of deionized water to form a homogeneous solution. This solution was kept under magnetic stirring with subsequent addition of ethylene glycol as surfactant at room temperature [13]. Afterwards, freshly prepared saturated sodium hydroxide solution was added to the mixture to adjust the pH to 12, and the whole mixture solution were continuously stirred for 45 min until a homogeneous solution is obtained. This was then poured into a 100 ml Teflon beaker and placed inside a hydrothermal autoclave and heated for 20 h at 180 °C. Finally, it was allowed to cool to room temperature naturally. Then, the solid powder was separated and washed with distilled water and dried. This dried powder was then heat treated at 900 °C for 10 h in a furnace to obtain the final product. Final products of Sr1-xZnxFe12O19 (x = 0–0.5, step of 0.1) samples such as SrFe12O19, Sr0.9Zn0.1Fe12O19, Sr0.8Zn0.2Fe12O19, Sr0.7Zn0.3Fe12O19, Sr0.6Zn0.4Fe12O19, and Sr0.5Zn0.5Fe12O19are labelled as SF, SZ1, SZ2, SZ3, SZ4 and SZ5, respectively.

Polycrystalline samples of BaFe12-xAxO19 (x = 0.1 and A = Ru4+ or Re4+) and BaFe12-xM2xO19 (x = 0.05; and M = (Ru4+, Re4+)) were prepared using the solid-state reaction method. The starting powders of BaCO3, Fe2O3, RuO2, and ReO2 with a purity > 98 % (Sigma-AldrichBrazil), were mixed in the desired stoichiometry. The stoichiometric mixtures were milled for 8 h to obtain finer particles and then calcined in air at 1000 °C for 8 h with a 20°C/min heating rate. The calcined powders were ground for 4 h and immediately sieved. After that, some amounts of the powders were pressed at 2.6 ton/cm2 in a 10 mm diameter disk-shaped samples and sintered at 1100 °C for 4 h, with a 10°C/min heating rate. The specific chemical formulas for each sample were: BaFe12O19 (BaM), BaFe11.9Ru0.1O19 (BaMRu), BaFe11.9Re0.1O19 (BaMRe), and BaFe11.9Ru0.05Re0.05O19 (BaMRuRe). The total value of x = 0.1 for doping and co-doping was selected using the criterion of the solubility limit. The synthesis process follows the chemical equations: BaCO3+ (5.95) Fe2O3+ (0.1) AO2 → BaFe11.9A0.1O19+CO2+ 0.025O2, (1) with A = Ru or Re, and for (Ru, Re) co-doping is BaCO3+ (5.95)Fe2O3 + (0.05)RuO2 + (0.05)ReO2 → BaFe11.9(Ru0.05Re0.05)O19+CO2+ 0.025O2. (2)

Sol-gel method was adapted to prepare M-type barium hexaferrite samples by considering analytical grade Ba(NO3)2 and Fe(NO3)3⋅9H2O as starting materials in stoichiometric ratios and dissolved in distilled water separately. These solutions were added into a beaker and while stirring on a hot plate, the citric acid solution was prepared separately by taking in the ratio of 1:1.2 w.r.t metal ion. Using a separating funnel with constant stirring the citric acid solution was added drop wise to the resultant solution and pH was maintained between 6.5 and 7.0 by adding ammonia solution. This solution was heated on a hot plate (90 °C) till the solution reached to one third of its value and later ethylene glycol was added in the ratio of 1: 2 and stirred for 30 min. The heating is continued and burns automatically giving rise to a foamy brown mass with the evaluation of gases. The mass is collected and grounded for 1 hr in an agate mortar and calcined at 700 °C/3h and the powders were made into circular pellets of 10 mm diameter. The pellets were sintered in a microwave furnace with a soaking time of 30 min by sintering at four different temperatures i.e., 750 °C, 850 °C, 950 °C & 1050 °C and cooled to room temperature.
Journal: Journal of Magnetism and Magnetic Materials

Synthesis_Procedure: Here, the sol-gel approach was chosen, as the technique yields particles that are finer in size [20,27]. In sol-gel processes, nitrates or oxides are typically employed as precursors. Every precursor was dissolved in double distilled water (DDW). To synthesize SrFe12O19, the precursors analytical grade Strontium Nitrate (Sr(NO3)2) (98 % SRL) and Ferric nitrate nonahydrate (Fe(NO3)3.9H2O) (98 % Sigma-Aldrich) were chosen. The reaction is, Sr(NO3)2 + Fe(NO3)3.9H2O→SrFe12O19 + H2O + N2 + O2 Additionally, a few other chemicals were added along with them that serve as secondary reagents. Citric acid (C6H8O7.H2O) (99.5 % SigmaAldrich), being a chelating agent, acts as a fuel thereby enhancing the rate of reaction for the synthesis of hexaferrite [33]. With that being said, it has to be noted that a complex precursor solution was produced when citric acid combined with metal ions, facilitating the production of finer particles and accurate stoichiometry [34]. The molar ratio of citric acid: metal ion was 1:1. Subsequently, ethylene glycol, C2H6O2(99.8 % Sigma-Aldrich), was mixed into the solution as a gelation agent. This promotes the formation of uniform and viscous gel, which guarantees a homogenous distribution of nanoparticles [35]. Ammonia solution NH4OH (30 % Sigma-Aldrich), serves as a pH buffer by maintaining the pH of the solution at a slightly basic level, which is required for producing the desired hexaferrite phase [28,34]. The solution was mixed and heated at 90 °C till the gel formation and raised to 150 °C till they undergo auto-combustion yielding SrFe12O19 and BaFe12O19 powders respectively. Analytical grade Barium Nitrate (Ba(NO3)2) (99 SRL) and Ferric nitrate nonahydrate (Fe(NO3)3.9H2O) (98 % Sigma-Aldrich) were opted as primary reagents for BaFe12O19 synthesis. Ba(NO3)2 + Fe(NO3)3.9H2O→BaFe12O19 + H2O + N2 + O2 The same procedures were followed for the reaction that gives out Barium hexaferrite. Each material was divided into 2 batches, ground well using a mortar and pestle, and compressed into a rectangular plate using a hydraulic press. For conventional sintering, both SrFe12O19 and BaFe12O19 powders were pre-sintered at 800 °C for 3 h followed by a final sintering at 1150 °C for 2 h in a conventional box furnace. A heating rate of 5 °C/min was maintained during the process. In the case of microwave sintering, plates were pre-sintered at 800 °C for 20 min and then annealed at 1150 °C for 20 min in a microwave furnace at a rate of 30 °C/min. It has been reported that sintering at 1000 °C or below results in samples with incomplete crystallization and smaller grain size. On the other side, temperatures beyond 1300 °C cause thermal decomposition and the formation of unnecessary secondary phases. A longer period is observed to cause the melting of the materials and thermal runaways. Hence, the time period of 20 min for microwave sintering was adopted [25]. The plate was crushed, ground again to powders after pre-sintering, and remoulded into the same shape before going through the final sintering in each case to ensure uniform particle size distribution and enhance mechanical properties. The synthesis process was repeated with temperature optimization until consistent powder yields were achieved from the same amount of precursors, and reproducible density was confirmed through XRD analysis.

In this experiment, BaFe12-2xCuxSnxO19 (x = 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75) ferrite ceramics were synthesized via the solid-state reaction method. In the first step, high-purity BaCO3 (99.8 %), Fe2O3 (99.5 %), CuO (99 %), and SnO2 (99.9 %) were used as raw materials. These powders were precisely weighed according to the required stoichiometric ratios. In the second step, the weighed powders were placed into a ball milling jar, with deionized water added for wetting. The mixture was then subjected to planetary ball milling at a rotational speed of 250 rpm for 12 h to ensure uniformity. In the third step, the homogenized slurry obtained after ball milling was dried in an oven at 60 °C. The dried powder was subsequently ground and pre-sintered in a muffle furnace at 1000 °C for 3 h. In the fourth step, the pre-sintered powder was finely ground, wetted with ethanol, and subjected to secondary ball milling in a planetary ball mill for an additional 12 h. In the fifth step, the milled slurry was dried in an oven at 60 °C. The dried powder was then uniformly mixed with 10 wt% polyvinyl alcohol (PVA) and 5 wt% deionized water. In the sixth step, the mixed powder was compacted into cylindrical shapes under a pressure of 12 MPa, followed by crushing and grinding into finer particles. In the seventh step, the ground powder was sieved using a dual-layer mesh screen, with an upper mesh of 120 and a lower mesh of 80, to obtain granulated sample powders. In the eighth step, the powder retained on the 80-mesh sieve was selected and pressed into disc-shaped samples under a pressure of 4 MPa. In the ninth step, the disc-shaped samples were sintered in a muffle furnace at 1100 °C for 6 h, followed by gradual cooling to room temperature under ambient air conditions.

BaCaM doped with copper and zirconium was prepared by SGACM in which barium nitrate (2.09 g) and calcium nitrate (0.47 g), and appropriate quantities of copper nitrate and zirconium nitrate were dissolved in distilled water in a 1000 ml beaker. Citric acid was added (1:1.5 mol ratio with respect to nitrates) under constant stirring. The precursor solution was adjusted to pH 7 by addition of ammonia solution, and the temperature was subsequently increased to 95–98°C for several hours. When the solution was converted to a gel, self-combustion was initiated by increasing the temperature to 200°C for 1 h. The grayish black powder obtained was then calcined at 900°C in an electric furnace for 6 h. After calcination, 1 g of barium calcium M-type polycrystalline powder was thoroughly mixed with 2 mL of a 2% PVA solution. After drying, the powder was crushed, sieved, and then compressed into 10 mm pellets using 7000 kg of pressure. Further, to eliminate any excess PVA, the pellets were sintered in crucibles for one hour at 1000°C. Details of chemicals used for the synthesis of Zr and Cu doped ferrites are listed in Table 1.

Synthesis_Procedure: Ba0.5Sr0.5Fe12–xCrxO19, where 0.5 ≤ x ≤ 3, solid solutions were synthesized at a step of 0.5 by a solidphase method from the Fe2O3 and Cr2O3 oxides and the BaCO3 and SrCO3 carbonates (special purity grade). The initial reagents were mixed in stoichiometric ratios according to Table 1. Mixing with simultaneous grinding was performed in a planetary mill at a rotation speed of 300 rpm for 5 h with the addition of ethanol. The ratio of the powder to zirconia grinding balls 7 mm in diameter was 1 : 1. The prepared mixture of the oxides and carbonates was then pressed on a hydraulic press into pellets 2 cm in diameter at a force of 5 t/cm2. The Sr1-xLaxFe12-xCoxO19 (x = 0, 0.2 & 0.3) (SLFCO) samples were synthesized using a conventional solidstate synthesis method. Analytical reagent-grade chemicals, including S rCO 3 (purity 99.9%), F e 2O 3 (purity > 95%), La2O3 (purity 99.9%), and Co3O4 (purity 99.9%), procured from Sigma-Aldrich, were employed as received. The initial reagents were meticulously measured using a high-precision analytical balance (Sartorius CPA225D, Germany) according to stoichiometric proportions, and the powder mixture was rollmilled with zirconia balls in isopropyl alcohol (IPA) for 24 h. The resulting slurry was heated and stirred at 90 °C until all IPA had evaporated. The mixed powders were then ground and uniformly mixed using an agate mortar and pestle. The as-synthesized precursor powder was calcined in an alumina crucible at 1050 °C for 4 h, at a ramping rate of 2 °C/min. After calcination, the powder underwent high-energy ball milling in a Fritsch Pulverisette 5 planetary mill, employing zirconia vials and 3 mm balls, with IPA as the milling medium. The powder-to-ball ratio was maintained at 1:10 and milling was performed for 6 h at 550 rpm. After ball milling, the calcined powder was dried at 90 °C to remove the IPA. The dried ball-milled powder was then uniaxially pressed into pellets of 8 mm diameter at 320 MPa. These pellets were sintered at 1050 °C, 1150 °C, 1250 °C and 1300 °C for 2 h in a conventional resistive heating furnace with a heating rate of 1 °C/min. The sintered pellets exhibited theoretical densities of ~ 68% at 1050 °C, ~ 84% at 1150 °C, ~ 92% at 1250 °C, and ~ 94% at 1300 °C for x = 0, 0.2 and 0.3 samples.
