Synthesis_Procedure: Crystals of Zn-substituted barium hexaferrites were grown from flux [42] composed of iron oxide (g-Fe2O3), zinc oxide (ZnO), barium carbonate (BaCO3) and sodium carbonate (Na2CO3) of 99.5% purity. Compositions of the batches are listed in Table 1. The initial mixture was ground in an agate mortar, filled into a 30 mL platinum crucible and placed in a resistive furnace. The details can be found elsewhere [43,44]. Heating was controlled by a type B thermocouple and a precision thermocontroller RIF-101. The furnace was maintained at 1260 °C for 4 h followed by cooling to 900 °C with a rate of 4.5 K/h. The solidified material after cooling to room temperature was leached in hot nitric acid to separate the crystals.

M-type, pure and yttrium substituted BaM hexaferrites with general formula BaYxFe12-xO19 (0.0≤x≤1.0) were prepared by facile ceramic method. The chemicals Fe2O3, Ba(CH3COO)2, Y2O3 and B2O3 used for the synthesis are analytically grade, purchased from Merck and applied directly without further purification. The stoichiometric amounts of Fe2O3, Ba(CH3COO)2 and Y2O3 precursors were weighed, mixed and well grinded in an agate mortar. The molar ratio of Fe/Ba was set to 12. Additive boron oxide B2O3 (1% mol) was added to the mixture in order to reduce the firing temperature requirement. The precursors were pre-calcinated at 400 oC for 3 h, cooled, grinded again and finally sintered at 1100 oC for 1 h.

First, an appropriate amount of barium acetate, ferric nitrate, lead nitrate dissolved in 50 ml deionized water by constant stirring at 60 °C and then citric acid was added to the mixture solution of Ba2+, Pb2+ and Fe3+ to chelate these ions. The molar ratio of citric acid to metal ions used was 1:1. Ammonia solution was added drop by drop to adjust the pH value to 12, which resulted in the co-precipitation of a gel like cake. Obtained gel was dried at 100 °C for 24 h, by increasing the temperature up to 250 °C, then dried gel were combusted to form brown loose powders. Finally, the precursor was calcined at temperature 1200 °C for 2 h duration to get the hexagonal phase of Ba1−xPbxFe12O19 (x=0.0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4).

The traditional method of solid-state reaction was used in this paper to prepare Ba(CoZr)xFe12-2xO19 (BFCZO-x, x = 0.2, 0.4, 0.6) ceramics. The starting materials were analytical-grade Fe2O3, BaCO3, CoO, and ZrO2. These materials were placed in agate milling containers with anhydrous ethanol as solvent and milled for 24 h at 250 rpm. BFCZO-x ceramics were calcined at 1100 °C for 4 h and milled. The powders were then ground with polyvinyl alcohol (PVA) in a mortar to prepare samples of 8 mm diameter and 1–2 mm thickness. To make PVA volatile, the samples were placed in an electric furnace at a temperature of 600 °C for 3 h. Finally, the pellets were sintered at 1190–1200 °C for 4 h in air atmosphere.

Synthesis_Procedure: In the present work, analytical grade BaCO3, Fe2O3 and Al2O3 were used to prepare BaFe12-xAlxO19, (x = 0.0 - 2.5) by solid state synthesis method. Precursors were weighed in stoichiometric composition and wet mixed for 3 hours using planetary ball mill. RPM and ball-to-charge ratio were fixed to 200 and 2:1 respectively. As-mixed powders were calcined at 1150 oC for 3 hours in a resistance furnace. Heating and cooling rate were fixed to 2 °C/minute. To prepare thick films, as synthesized powder were mixed with PVB (Polyvinyl butyral) binder and screen printed on Al2O3 substrate using a screen of 175 µm thickness. Asprinted films were sintered at 1250 °C for one hour in ambient atmosphere. For the study fine powder where compacted in a rectangular shape with dimension 22.86x10.16x2.1 mm3 under a pressure of 50 Mpa. As prepared pellets were sintered at 1250⁰ C for 1h .
Journal: Journal of Magnetism and Magnetic Materials

Synthesis_Procedure: An aqueous solution of Sr(NO3)2·4H2O and Fe(NO3)3·9H2O was mixed, with Sm(NO3)3·6H2O and Co(NO3)2·6H2O added in for the substitutions. The ratio [Sr2+ + Sm3+]/[Fe3+ + Co2+] was kept equal to 1/10.5, as it is reported that the excess strontium helps in the limitation of unwanted secondary phases such as SrFe2O4 [13]. An aqueous solution of NaOH was infused keeping the ratio [OH−]/[NO3−] equal or greater than 2. Finally, the solution was stirred at 700 rpm for 2 h at 85 °C and filtered. The precipitate was washed and dried for 16 h at 95 °C. The samples were pressed into pellets with a 10 t hydraulic press. The pellets were calcined in air for 2 h at a range of temperatures (800– 1200 °C) in order to study the formation of the hexaferrite phase and achieve the best hard magnetic properties. After the ideal calcination conditions were identified, the material was sintered once again from the chemical precipitate, using the molten flux method, in order to investigate the effect of the method in the magnetic properties. Here, instead of pressing the powder into a pellet, the powder was mixed in a ball mill with analytical grade NaCl with a mass ratio of 1:2 and sintered at the same conditions in an alumina crucible. Afterwards, the powder was washed to remove any remaining NaCl and dried for 16 h at 95 °C.

Iron oxide (c-Fe2O3), cobalt oxide (CoO), nickel oxide (NiO), barium carbonate (BaCO3) and sodium carbonate (Na2CO3) of 99.5–99.8% purity as flux were used as starting materials. The composition of the batch (Table 1) was chosen using literature data for growth of non-substituted M-type barium hexaferrite BaFe12O19 [34]. The initial mixture was ground in an agate mortar and filled into a 30 mL platinum crucible. The crucible was placed in a vertical tube Kanthal resistive furnace equipped with a type B thermocouple as described elsewhere [46,47]. To homogenize the educts, the furnace was maintained at 1260 °C for 3 h. After that a Pt wire was placed into the solution at constant temperature. Pt wire worked as cool spot for heat sink and crystallization center. On the wire surface crystals grow spontaneously, having sizes of up to 15 mm. As soon as temperature was constant the main solute remained in solution and mass yield was 5–10%. The solvent evaporation losses were 1–2%. These crystals were separated from the solidified melt by leaching in hot nitric acid to remove all additional phases (e.g. NaFeO2 next to Na2CO3 and BaCO3).

The starting materials, barium nitrate Ba(NO3)2 (99.9%), iron nitrate extra pure Fe(NO3)3, copper(II) acetate monohydrate Cu(CH3·COO)2·H2O, citric acid (C6H8O7), and ammonia solution were obtained from Sigma-Aldrich and used as received. Stoichiometric amounts of Fe(NO3)3, Ba(NO3)2 and Cu(CH3COO)2·H2O (molar ratio of citric acid to metal ions = 1/2) were dissolved in 30 ml of deionized water. Synthesis_Procedure: The appropriate molar ratios of analytical grade starting materials (BaCO3, Fe2O3, and V2O3) were used to synthesize the desired samples. We used 1:11 as the ratio between Ba: Fe which is the optimal ratio to give a single phase of undoped BaFe12O19 [56]. The powder precursors were mixed in zirconia containers and ball-milled by zirconia balls in a Fritch Pulverissette-7 ball mill for 16 h at 250-rpm rotational speed. The wet milling was carried out in an acetone bath, with powder to ball mass ratio of 1:14, and powder to acetone ratio of 5:8. The wet powder was then left to dry in air, and then part of it was pressed into a disc of 1.2 cm in diameter and ~ 0.15 cm in thickness under a force of 5 tons. The discs were sintered in air at T ≥ 1100 οC for 2 h.

Synthesis_Procedure: All chemicals used are of reagent-grade purity (purity >99.9 %). The BaNdxFe12−xO19 was prepared by initial planetary ball milling of the precursors and calcining subsequently. In a typical synthesis (BaFe12O19), 1.18 g BaC2O4·2H2O, 9.71 g FeC2 O·2H2O, and 10 ml ethanol were added to a stainless steel ball milling tank of 100 ml. The mass ratio of the sample to the stainless steel ball is about 1/15. Samples were milled at room temperature for 30 min. The grinding velocity was about 350 circles/min. BaFe12O19 precursor was obtained after being dried at 80 °C in air for 5 h. A similar synthesis procedure was used to synthesize other BaNdxFe12−xO19 precursor. Finally, the BaNdxFe12−xO19 precursor was calcined over 950 °C for 3 h at a heating rate of 2 °C min−1 in air to produce hexagonal BaNdxFe12−xO19 .

Synthesis_Procedure: All the samples of Ba-hexaferrites Ba1−xLaxFe12−xZnxO19 (x = 0.0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4) were synthesized by co-precipitation and citrate combustion process. High-purity reagent grade raw materials without further purification were used for preparing the samples. These samples have been prepared according to the following chemical equation: (1 − x)Ba(CH3COO)2 + xLa(NO3)3·6H2O + (12 − X)Fe(NO3)3·9H2O + xZn(NO3)2·6H2O —(Citric acid/ammonia solution)→ Ba(1−x)LaxFe(12−x)ZnxO19 According to B a 1−xLa xFe 12−xZn xO 19 stoichiometric amounts of Barium acetate (Ba(CH3COO)2), Lanthanum nitrate hexa-hydrate (La(NO3)3⋅6H2O), ferric nitrate Nonahydrate (Fe(NO3)3⋅9H2O) and Zinc nitrate hexa-hydrate (Zn(NO3)2⋅6H2O) and citric acid were dissolved in deionized water. The precipitation reaction occurred after adding drop by drop ammonia solution in mixed metal solution and during this process, the pH value of the solution was adjusted to pH-12. For these sample preparations, citric acid and the metal ions have been used in 1:1 ratio. The transparent solutions were heated at 80 °C with regular stirring. After heating, these transparent solutions were converted into the gels. Further, the brown ferrite powder was obtained by the gel precursors combusted at 250 °C. The brown ferrite powders were ground and calcined at 1200 °C for 2 h. After that, pellets were formed using Hydraulic pressure machine at 5 MPa/cm2 and finally, these pellets were annealed at 200 °C for 2 h in a furnace.

Powder precursors of BaFe12-2xVxCuxO19 (x = 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4) were synthesized by ball milling the stoichiometric ratios of analytical grade BaCO3, Fe2O3, V2O5, Cu2O. The appropriate amounts of these material were carefully weighed, and charged into the zirconia vessels of the Fritch Pulveressette-7 ballmill. Wet-milling of the powder by zirconia balls in an acetone bath (Powder to acetone mass ratio = 5:8) was performed for 16 h at a rotational speed of 250 rpm, with a powder to ball mass ration of 1:14. The resulting muddy mixture was dried in air, and pressed into disc-shaped pellets 1.5 cm in diameter and ~ 1.0 mm in thickness under a force of 5 tons. The disc was then sintered at 1200°C for 2 h.

Synthesis_Procedure: Powder precursors of barium hexaferrites with stoichiometry consistent with the chemical formula BaFe12-4xMoxZn3xO19 were prepared from high purity (~99%) powders of BaCO3, Fe2O3, ZnO and MoO2 (Sigma-Aldrich made). The barium to metal molar ratio was 1:11.5, and the mixing and homogenization of the powder precursors was achieved by using a planetary ball mill (Fritch Pulverisette 7). The milling cups and balls were made of zirconia, and the powder-to-ball mass ratio was 1:14 to ensure effective grinding and obtain homogenous powders. Wet milling of the powder precursors in an acetone bath (8 ml for each 5 grams of the powder) was performed for 16 hours at a rotational speed of 250 rpm. The wet powder was then left in the container overnight to dry at room temperature, and subsequently collected in clean glass vials. About 1 g of the powder was mixed with an adhesive agent of 2% wt. of polyvinyl alcohol (PVA) and then dry-pressed into disc-shape pellet (1.5 cm in diameter) in a stainless steel die under a 4 ton force. The discs were then sintered at temperatures ranging from 1100°C to 1300°C for 2 h in air.

In the current work, BaFe12-2xCuxMnxO19 (x = 0.00, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75, and 1.00) were prepared by wet grinding using a high energy ball mill (Fritsch Pulverisette-7). The powder-to-ball mass ratio was 1:14, and the grinding was maintained for 16 hours at 250 rpm rotational speed, with grinding periods of 10 min. separated by 5 min. pause periods to avoid overheating during the grinding process. The molar ratio of (Fe + Cu + Mn) to Ba was chosen to be 11.5, in accordance with the conclusions of a recent study concerned with the optimal ratio required for the preparation of a pure BaM phase [32]. The precursor powder mixtures were pressed, under a pressure of 43 kN/cm2, into small disks (~ 12 mm in diameter and ~ 1.5 mm in thickness), and then sintered at 1100ο C for 2 h in air.

The stoichiometric amounts of Fe (NO3)3·9H2O, Sr(NO3), Ca (NO3)2·4H2O, La(NO3)3·6H2O, and Cr (NO3)3·9H2O were dissolved in deionized water. Molar ratio stabilized at (Sr + La + Ca): (Fe + Cr) = 1:12, with, [Sr2+:La3+] = [0.85 − x:0.15], x = (0, 0.1, 0.3, and 0.5), [Fe:Cr] = [11.5:0.5]. After dissolving them in deionized water, citric acid was introduced into the solution by keeping the molar ratio of metal ions to citric acid at 1:1. Ammonium hydroxide was then gradually added to the solution to adjust pH at about 7. The temperature was adjusted at 80 °C and stirred for 2.5 h. As the gel was burned and changed to the sol during an auto-combustion route, the powder was then calcinated at 1030 °C for 2.5 h. The complete reaction proceeds as the following: (0.85 − x)Sr (NO3)2 + 0.15 La(NO3)3⋅6H2O + xCa (NO3)2⋅4H2O + (11.5) Fe(NO3)3⋅9H2O + 0.5 Cr(NO3)3⋅9H2O + C6H8O7 + NH4OH = Sr0.85−xLa0.15CaxFe11.5Cr0.5O19 + NH4NO3 + CO2 + H2O.

After dissolving them in deionized water, citric acid was introduced into the solution by keeping the molar ratio of metal ions to citric acid at 1:1. As the gel was burned and changed to the sol during an auto-combustion route, the powder was then calcinated at 1030 °C for 2.5 h. Synthesis_Procedure: Improved solid phase method was employed to fabricate the La3+–Ni2+ substituted strontium ferrites with chemical composition of Sr1−xLaxFe12−xNixO19 (x = 0–0.35). Starting materials of SrCO3 (99.5 wt%), Fe2O3 (99 wt%), La2O3 (99.99 wt%), and Ni2O3 (99.5 wt%) powders were weighed and mixed by ball milling (BM, QM-3SP4) at 300 r/min for 2 h with ethanol as medium. After drying and sifting, the mixed powders were calcined at 1250 °C for 2 h by high temperature sintering furnace (KSL-1400X) and then crushed by BM at 400 r/min for 4 h with 3 wt% Bi2O3 (99.9 wt%) to get the low temperature sintering powders with average particle size of 0.8–1.0 μm. The powders were pressed into disks with 6 wt% polyvinyl alcohol binder with a diameter of 12 mm at 45 MPa by oil press machine (Y41-10), and then sintered at 870 °C for 30 min using microwave sintering furnace (GER-M2) with working frequency of 2.45 GHz and output power of 2 kW. Subsequently, the annealing at 750 °C for 12 h was carried out for the sintered samples to release the internal stress [35].

Synthesis_Procedure: BaFe12−xNixO19 hexaferrites with nickel content x = 0, 0.3 and 0.5 were synthesized by the conventional solid state mixed oxide route. Stoichiometric amounts of pure and dried BaCO3 (Riadel-de Haen, 99%), Fe2O3 (UniChem, 99.5%) and NiO (Grey/ Green British House Drug Ltd., 99%) were mixed in ethanol for 4 h and then calcined at 900°C in air atmosphere for 5 h. Calcined powder was milled with the aid of ethanol for 3 h. The resulting powders were converted into pellets using a hydraulic press by applying a force of 6000 lb and then sintered at 1300°C for 2 h.

The chemicals used for the synthesis of SrFe12−xNixO19 nanoparticle are as follows: Iron nitrate pentahydrate (Fe(NO3)3·9H2O), nickel nitrate hexahydrate Ni(NO3)2·6H2O, and strontium nitrate anhydrous (Sr(NO3)2 ) as inorganic reactants, ammonium hydroxide as a neutralizing agent, citric acid as chelating agent, and deionized water as solvent. The starting materials were of high-purity compounds and used without further purification. In this work, SrFe12−xNixO19 (x = 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1) hexagonal ferrites were prepared by sol-gel auto-combustion method as follows: first, the inorganic precursors including Sr(NO3)2 , Fe(NO3)3·9H2O and Ni(NO3)2·6H2O in desired proportions corresponding to their stoichiometric formula (SrFe12−xNixO19) were dissolved in deionized water by stirring on a hotplate at 50°C. Then temperature was increased slowly to 70°C and citric acid was added to the obtained sol with molar ratio of citric acid to total metal ions as 1:1. The resulting mixture was stirred for 30 min and afterward, the pH of solution was adjusted at 7 by adding ammonium hydroxide. Subsequently, the sol was heated on a hotplate with continuous stirring to evaporate the water until a highly viscous brown residue was formed. In the final step of the sol-gel auto-combustion process, the viscous residue was heated at 250°C for 1 h and then the obtained dark brown ashes were calcined at 1000°C for 5 h at a rate of 5°C/min.

Synthesis_Procedure: The sol–gel auto-combustion method has been used to fabricate the nanoparticles. First, the stoichiometric amounts of the raw materials BaCl2, CoCl2, MgCl2, ZrO(NO3)2, TiCl4, and Fe(NO3)3 were added to the sufficient amount of deionized water. Next, citric acid in the ratio of 1:1 to the total moles of nitrate and chloride ions were added to the solution. The solution was then neutralized by adding ammonia solution dropwise to the mixed solution. Along with continuous stirring, the solution was then heated at 80 °C to form a viscous brown gel. Increasing the temperature at this stage caused the ignition of the gel. When ignited points were observed, the dried gel burnt in a self-propagating combustion process until all the gels were burnt out completely to form fine powders. Finally, the obtained powders were calcined at 900 °C for two hours.

Next, citric acid in the ratio of 1:1 to the total moles of nitrate and chloride ions were added to the solution. The solution was then neutralized by adding ammonia solution dropwise to the mixed solution. Along with continuous stirring, the solution was then heated at 80 °C to form a viscous brown gel. Increasing the temperature at this stage caused the ignition of the gel. When ignited points were observed, the dried gel burnt in a self-propagating combustion process until all the gels were burnt out completely to form fine powders. Finally, the obtained powders were calcined at 900 °C for two hours.
Journal: Journal of Sol-Gel Science and Technology

Synthesis_Procedure: Samples of pure barium nanohexaferrites (BaFe12O19) and doped samples of nickel barium nanohexaferrites (BaNixFe(12-x)O19) with x = 0.01, 0.05, 0.1 for nickel concentration to be 1, 5 and 10%, respectively, are synthesized using the chemical co-precipitation method followed by calcination at 800°C for 4 h. A part of the sample of pure barium nanohexaferrite is calcined at 600°C and is named as Pure600 and the other calcined at 800°C is named as Pure800. For pure sample, stoichiometric quantities of barium chloride di-hydrated (BaCl2·2H2O: Fisher Scientific, Purity min. 99%) and ferric chloride hexa-hydrated (FeCl3·6H2O: SD Fine Chemical, Purity min. 97%) having Fe/Ba molar ratio of 12:1 are mixed homogeneously in distilled water with continuous stirring for a few hours to form a consistent and homogeneous solution. An alkaline solution of 10 M NaOH is added drop by drop to this salt solution while the pH is checked continuously and the stirring is sustained. With the further addition of NaOH, the pH value increases and the burette is closed as soon as the pH of 12 is achieved (Iqbal & Ashiq, 2008). The stirring is still continued to maintain the homogeneity of the mixture. At this point, dark brown precipitates are formed which are further filtered out and washed many times using de-ionized water and later washed with ethanol to get rid of the excess amount of chlorine and other by-products. Drying of the washed precipitates is done in an oven at 100°C for 24 h in order to properly remove the water from it. The dried samples are then grinded properly to prepare the powdered form. Further, in a muffle furnace, the calcination at 800°C for 4 h is done followed by a final grinding. For the nickel-doped barium nanohexaferrites, calcined at 800°C, a similar synthesis route is followed in which stoichiometric amount of NiCl2·6H2O (SDFCL; Purity: 97%) is used as an additional precursor at the first stage. The selection of 800°C as the calcination temperature for Ni-doped samples is done based on the results obtained for pure barium nanohexaferrite calcined at 800 and 600°C.

First, to produce samples of BaFe12O19, aqueous mixtures of barium (II) nitrate (Ba(No3)2), iron (III) nitrate (Fe(NO3)3) and NaOH solution (0.98 M) were prepared by the hydrothermal method. The resulting suspensions were sealed in an autoclave cell and heated for the required duration and then cooled to room temperature. To produce powders, the suspension was washed repeatedly using deionized water until no NaCl was detectable, dried at 100 in an oven, calcined at 800°C, 900°C, and 1000°C for 2 h at a heating rate of 10°C/min and then free cooled to room temperature. The starting materials used for preparation of the samples were Fe(NO3)3.9H2O (Merck, 98%), Ba(No3)2 (Merck, 99%), Gd (NO3)3.6H2O (Aldrovich, 99.5%), Mn(NO3)2.4H2O (Merck, 98.5%), Co(NO3)2.6H2O (99%) and NaOH (Merck, 99%). In a typical experimental procedure, stoichiometric aqueous mixtures of barium nitrate (Ba(No3)2), cobalt nitrate (Co(NO3)2), manganese nitrate (Mn(NO3)2), gadolinium nitrate (Gd(NO3)3) and iron nitrate (Fe(NO3)3) were prepared with a total concentration of 0.1 mol L−1. These materials are mixed in compositions of Ba:(Fe + Mn + Gd + Co) = 1:12 with the nominal formula of Ba1−xGdxFe12−2y(MnCo)yO19 and a ratio of y = 2x, where x is equal to 0, 0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 0.9 and 1, prepared by the hydrothermal method. Stoichiometric amounts of the metal salts were weighed and mixed with distilled water for 30 min. Sodium hydroxide (NaOH) solution (0.98 M) as a precipitating agent was then added dropwise to the mixture to adjust the solution pH to 12 under vigorous stirring. At the same time the solution containing the precipitate was stirred for 2 h. The resulting suspensions were sealed in an autoclave cell at 200°C for 7 h and heated for the required duration and then cooled to room temperature. Finally to produce powders, the precipitates were washed three times with water by centrifuge to reduce the pH to 7 and remove remaining NaCl and NaOH, then dried at 100°C in an oven and calcined at 900°C in a programmed furnace for 2 h at a heating rate of 10°C/min and then free-cooled to room temperature.

The solid-state method techniques were used to synthesize the M-type SrLa hexaferrites with nominal compositions of Sr0.75La0.25Fe12.0-2x(ZrMn)xO19 (where x = 0.00, 0.15, 0.30, 0.45, 0.60, 0.75). Finally, to relieve the stress, the shattered particles were annealed in a muffle furnace at 760 °C for 1.5 h.

Ba(NO3)2·6H2O (≥ 99% Merck, India), Co(NO3)2.6H2O (≥ 98% Merck, India), Sm2O3 (≥ 99.9% Thomas Baker, Spain) Fe(NO3)2.9H2O (≥98% Merck, India) and C6H8O7 (≥99.5% Merck, India) of AR grade were used without further purification as a starting material for the synthesis of BaCo0.8SmxFe11.2 − xO19 (0.2≥x ≥0.6 in step of 0.2) nanoferrite. Double distilled water was used as a solvent. All the chemicals were weighed in proper stoichiometry and dissolved in 0.5 M solution of citric acid. The prepared solution was heated to boiling under constant refluxing/ stirring condition simultaneously converted to viscous form called xerogel. This xerogel was further heated until a brown fluffy mass was formed which ultimately collapsed to precursor powder. As there is no precipitation at any stage, therefore the problem of segregation of phases which generally occur in other synthesis processes like co-precipitation, did not take place in this process [20]. The precursor formed was then pre-sintered at 700 °C for 3 h and pressed in cylindrical shaped pellets. The powder and pellets were finally sintered at 900 °C.

A series of M-type barium hexaferrites with formula BaCexFe12 − xO19 (0 ≤ x ≤0.3) (BCFO) was prepared by the sol–gel auto combination method. Initially all AR grade metal nitrate Ba(NO3)2, Ce(NO3)3·6H2O and Fe(NO3)3·9H2O stoichiometric amount were dissolved in deionized water. Citric acid (C6H8O7) was then added into aqueous solution of metal nitrate. The metal nitrate to citric acid ratio was kept as 1:3 and then the pH of the mixed solution was kept at 8 by adding ammonia solution. The mixed solution was evaporated to dryness by heating at 80 °C on a hot plate with continuous stirring and finally formed a very viscous brown gel. This viscous brown gel was ignited by increasing the temperature up to 100 °C and the loose powder of the samples was obtained. Finally, the as burnt powder was annealed at 1000 °C for 6 h to obtain Ce substituted barium hexaferrite nanoparticles.
Journal: Journal of Magnetism and Magnetic Materials

Synthesis_Procedure: In this work the sol-gel method was adopted for synthesizing Ce substituted barium ferrite samples. Iron nitrate (Fe(NO3)3), barium nitrate (Ba(NO3)2), cerium oxide (CeO2), ethylenediamine tetraacetic acid (EDTA(C10H16N2O8), citric acid (C6H8O7), and ammonia solution were taken as the precursor materials and weighted according to the stoichiometric ratio. First EDTA was dissolved in deionized water under stirring and heating. Then iron nitrate, barium nitrate, and cerium nitrate were dissolved in deionized water under stirring at 40oC to form an aqueous solution. Citric acid and EDTA were then added in to the solution and molar ratio of EDTA and citric acid to total metal cations was adjusted at 1:1. The pH of the solution was adjusted around 7 using NH4OH. The solution was slowly evaporated at 80oC until becoming a highly viscose gel. Then temperature of the hot plate was increased to about 200oC to obtain a dried gel. Finally the dried gel powders were sintered in air at 1100oC for 3h.

Synthesis_Procedure: Barium hexaferrite nanoparticles substituted with Mg+2, Mn+2, Co+2 and Ti+4 cations, were prepared by adopting a co-precipitation method. To this end, stoichiometric amounts of the starting materials were dissolved in deionized water at 70 oC and stirred to form a homogenous solution. Afterwards, polyvinyl alcohol (2 wt. %) was added to the above solution as a surfactant. Then, NaOH (1.5 M) was gradually added to the solution until the pH value raised up to 13. The aqueous suspensions were further stirred again for 1 h to homogenize the system. The resulting gel then was washed several times with deionized water until the pH value of the solution became neutral. The solution was subsequently filtered and dried at 100 oC. Finally, the resulting powder was calcined at 950 oC for 2h.

Synthesis_Procedure: The raw materials used in the present work were purchased from Merck and were used as received. The pure barium hexaferrite and BaFe10.5-xAl1.5CrxO19 nanoparticles with different composition (x = 0, 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0) were prepared via autocombustion sol–gel method. A stoichiometric amounts of Ba(NO3)2, Fe(NO3)3·9H2O, Al(NO3)3·9H2O and Cr(NO3)3·9H2O were dissolved in deionized water and the mixture was vigorously stirred on a hotplate in 60 °C. Citric acid was weighed as a molar ratio of metal ions to citric acid of 1:5 and add into the solution. After dissolving the nitrate salts completely, the solution were allowed to cool down to room temperature and then ammoniac was added to adjust the pH value to ca. 7.0. These solution were slowly evaporated on a hotplate at 80 °C until a highly viscous residue dried gels were formed and then the viscous residue dried gels were heated at 250 °C to ignite with the formation of large amounts of gas, resulting in light weight voluminous powder. Before annealing, the resulting precursor powders was preheated to 450 °C for 1 h to decompose the organic precursor and volatile gases. Finally, the resulting precursor powders were calcined at 950 °C for 2 h. The procedure for the synthesis of pure and substituted barium hexaferrite has been illustrated in Fig. 1.

A stoichiometric amounts of Ba(NO3)2, Fe(NO3)3·9H2O, Al(NO3)3·9H2O and Cr(NO3)3·9H2O were dissolved in deionized water and the mixture was vigorously stirred on a hotplate in 60 °C. Citric acid was weighed as a molar ratio of metal ions to citric acid of 1:5 and add into the solution. After dissolving the nitrate salts completely, the solution were allowed to cool down to room temperature and then ammoniac was added to adjust the pH value to ca. 7.0. These solution were slowly evaporated on a hotplate at 80 °C until a highly viscous residue dried gels were formed and then the viscous residue dried gels were heated at 250 °C to ignite with the formation of large amounts of gas, resulting in light weight voluminous powder. Before annealing, the resulting precursor powders was preheated to 450 °C for 1 h to decompose the organic precursor and volatile gases. Finally, the resulting precursor powders were calcined at 950 °C for 2 h. The procedure for the synthesis of pure and substituted barium hexaferrite has been illustrated in Fig. 1.

High purity raw materials, FeCl3.6H2O (Merck, >98%), BaCl2.2H2O (Merck, >99%), CoCl2.6H2O (Merck, >99%), MnCl2.4H2O (Merck, >99%), MgCl2.6H2O (Aldrich, >99%), ZnCl2 (Merck, >98%), TiCl4 (Aldrich, >99%), NaOH (Merck, >99%) and absolute ethanol (Merck, >99.95) were used as the starting materials. First, to produce the single-phase barium hexaferrite, pure BaM (without any dopant, x = 0) was synthesized with the four different Fe3+/Ba2+ molar ratios of 10, 8, 6, and 4. The XRD results showed that the single-phase barium hexaferrite was achieved only at a molar ratio of 4; therefore, two series of ferrites, including BaCoxMnxTi2xFe12-4xO19 (a) and BaMgxZnxTi2xFe12-4xO19 (b) with x = 0.0, 0.5, 0.7, and 0.9 were synthesized using this molar ratio. For this purpose, stoichiometric amounts of the metallic chlorides Ba2+, Fe3+, Co2+, Mn2+, Mg2+, Zn2+ and Ti4+ were dissolved into a mixture of deionized water and ethanol (50/50, Vol%) as the solvent for each specific ferrite. The metal ion solutions were heated to 70 ̊C, a 2M solution of sodium hydroxide was gradually added until the pH solution reached a value of 13, and it was stirred continuously to form a brownish yellow precipitate. This precipitate was washed with deionized water several times to remove any unwanted impurities and chloride ions. The complete removal of chloride ions was confirmed from the pH and conductivity measurements of the deionized water and the wash effluent. After washing, the precipitate was mixed with ethanol to remove the surface adsorbed water molecules which otherwise might have led to agglomeration of the particles during the drying and subsequent processing [32]. The precipitate was then filtered and dried at 100 ̊C for 6 hours. The dried precipitate was ground in an ordinary porcelain mortar and then was calcined at 1000 ̊C for 5 h with a heating rate of 5 ̊C/min. Before choosing 1000 ̊C as appropriate temperature for calcination, we synthesized some samples of pure BaM at 900, 1000 and 1200 ̊C. The XRD results showed that there was poor crystallization at 900 ̊C while the undesirable α-Fe2O3 phase (an antiferrnomagnetic phase) was created at 1200 ̊C.

High purity (>98%) BaCO3, Fe2O3, Cu2O were used as starting materials to prepare the system BaFe12−xCuxO19 (x = 0.0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8). The barium to iron molar ratio of Ba/Fe = 1:11.5 was found to be optimal for the synthesis of a single M-type phase in the undoped sample, and the desired Fe (x) fraction was substituted by Cu in the doped samples. The appropriate amounts of these materials were weighted carefully, and then added directly to the ball-mill (Fritch-Pulverissette-7) vessels. 8 mL of acetone was added to each 5 g of the precursor powders for better suspension of the powder grains between the crushing zirconium oxide balls, and more efficient grinding. The powder-to-balls mass ratio was 1:14. The grinding was maintained for 16 h at 250-rpm rotational speed, and the grinding period was performed in intervals of 10 min each separated by 5 min pause periods to avoid overheating during the grinding process. The resulting powder was left in the vessels to dry in air at room temperature. About 0.8 g of each dry powder was pressed into a disk of approximately 1 cm in diameter and 2 mm in thickness under a force of 5 t. The disks were then sintered at 1100 °C for periods of 2 h in air.

BaFe12 − xAlxO19 samples were prepared by ball milling appropriate mixtures of BaCO3, Fe2O3 and Al2O3 powders. The amount of each compound was determined for each particular stoichiometry of BaFe12 − xAlxO19 and then mixed in a ball milling cylinder. The mechanical alloying was carried out in a traditional ball mill for 96 h with the spin speed of 45 rpm, and the weight ratio of ball to powders was about 30:1. For the first 48 h we used stainless steel ball while the reminder of the ball milling process was accomplished using stabilized zirconia cylinders. After milling, the powders were pressed into cylinder pellets 1 cm in diameter and 0.5 cm in thickness. Calcination was then carried out for 48 h in air at 1000 °C.

The amount of each compound was determined for each particular stoichiometry of BaFe12 − xAlxO19 and then mixed in a ball milling cylinder. The mechanical alloying was carried out in a traditional ball mill for 96 h with the spin speed of 45 rpm, and the weight ratio of ball to powders was about 30:1. For the first 48 h we used stainless steel ball while the reminder of the ball milling process was accomplished using stabilized zirconia cylinders. After milling, the powders were pressed into cylinder pellets 1 cm in diameter and 0.5 cm in thickness. Calcination was then carried out for 48 h in air at 1000 °C.

Synthesis_Procedure: FeCl3·6H2O (Merck, >98%), SrCl2·6H2O (Merck, >99%), TiCl4 (Merck, >99%), ZnCl2·4H2O (Merck, >99%) and NaOH (Merck, >99%) were used as the starting materials to synthesize M-type hexaferrite powders with the compositions of SrFe12−xTix/2Znx/2O19 (where x varies from 0 to 2.5 in steps of 0.5) by means of co-precipitation technique. Stoichiometric amount of the salts were dissolved in distilled water to achieve aqueous solution; subsequently, NaOH (1 M) was gradually added while stirring so as to form the precipitate until the solution pH reached a value of 12. The aqueous suspensions were further stirred for another 1 h to homogenize the system. Having been filtered, the ferrite precursors were washed several times with distilled water, dried at 100 °C and calcined at 900 °C for 1 h. A high energy ball mill machine (SPEX Certprep-M8000) equipped with hardened steel balls was used in order to reduce the calcined powders particle size. The stearic acid, as a process control agent, was added in milling procedure. The ball to powder weight ratio of 10:1, shaking frequency of 50 Hz, and milling time of 1.5 h were applied during the process.

A series of Cr3+-doped SrCrxFe12–xO19 (x = 0.0, 0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 0.9) powders were prepared by the microwave–hydrothermal method. High-purity (99.9%) chemicals strontium nitrate [Sr(NO3)2·6H2O], ferric nitrate [Fe(NO3)2·9H2O], and chromium nitrate [Cr(NO3)3·9H2O] were carefully weighed and the molar ratio of powders adjusted to obtain the compositions SrCrxFe12−xO19 (x = 0.0, 0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 0.9). The powders were dissolved in deionized water, and NaOH was added to control pH ~12. The obtained brown precipitate was heated to 80°C for 30 min with constant stirring to obtain a homogeneous mixture. The mixture was then treated in a Teflon-lined vessel using a microwave digestion system (model MDS-2000; CEM Corp., Mathews, NC). This system uses 2.45-GHz microwaves and can operate at 0% to 100% of full power (1200 ± 50 W). The steam pressure in the system is controlled and can attain a maximum pressure of 200 psi, which is equivalent to 194°C based on steam tables. In the present study, all the compositions were synthesized at 200°C for 45 min. The reaction vessel was connected to a pressure transducer to monitor and control the pressure during synthesis. The time, pressure, and power were computer controlled. The obtained products were filtered, then washed repeatedly with deionized water, followed by freeze-drying overnight. The as-prepared powders were weighed, and the percentage yields were calculated from the expected total amount based on the solution concentration and volume and the amount that was actually crystallized. An average yield of 96% was obtained. The obtained powders were mixed with an appropriate amount of 2 wt.% polyvinyl alcohol as binder. Then, the powder was uniaxially pressed at pressure of 800 kg/cm2 to form green pellet specimens. The compacts were sintered at 950°C for 90 min using the microwave sintering method.

Synthesis_Procedure: SrFe12O19 NPs were prepared by following a sol–gel route similar to as reported by Singhal et al [11]. The starting materials were strontium nitrate (Sr(NO3)2), iron (III) nitrate nonahydrate (Fe(NO3)3 .9H2O), citric acid (CA) and ethylene glycol (EG). CA and EG were used as chelating and polymerization agents respectively. First, an appropriate amount of Sr3+ and Fe3+ salts and CA were dissolved in minimum amount of distilled water such that the molar ratio of CA to all metal cations was 1:1. EG was added to the solution with continuous stirring keeping the ratio of CA:EG as 60:40 (in mass proportion). The transparent solution was heated in a water bath at 110 °C with continuous stirring until a viscous brown colored gel had been obtained. The viscous gel was dried thoroughly under an IR lamp. The dried gel powder was crushed and annealed at different temperatures in the range 500–900 °C for 2 h to facilitate formation of the desired phase with required particle sizes.

The multi-walled carbon nanotubes were activated in an acid solution of concentrated nitric acid, sonicated for 5.5h. Afterwards, MWCNTs were dried at 90 o C . The Mn-Sn-Ti substituted strontium ferrite was fabricated by sol-gel method. In the sol gel technique, first, a strontium citrate solution is formed from stoichiometric amounts of strontium chloride (SrCl2.6H2O) and citric acid (C6H8O7) in the molar ratio 1.5:1. This was further mixed with a ferric chloride (FeCl3) in proportion for a set of compositions with Fe/Sr ratio of 12. The resultant homogeneous solution with pH=0.5 was recharged with TiCl4, SnCl4, MnCl2.2H2O to obtain the citrate complex of precursors. The prepared samples were calcined at 950 °C for 1h in air atmosphere. Using the sonication operation, the MWCNTs treated with HNO3 were dispersed in the acrylic acid and distilled water solution for 0.5h, then the strontium ferrite was added to the mixture and sonicated again for 0.5h. The composites with the 20% vol MWCNTs content were prepared and finally dried at 90 o C for 24h for further using.

The synthesis of Co–Zr-doped nanocrystalline M-type Bahexaferrites (x = 0.0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8, and 1.0) has been accomplished by self-combustion method. In this method, the reaction was carried out in the presence of urea as a fuel. Hydrated metal salts viz. Ba(NO3)2 , Co(NO3)2·6H2O, ZrO(NO3)2·6H2O, and Fe(NO3)3·9H2O were employed as starting material for their synthesis. Ferric nitrate and urea were dissolved in deionized water and mixed both in a ratio of 1:1.5, respectively. A stoichiometric amount of desired metal salts was added into the above solution and stirred for 2–3 h at 70 °C. The gel automatically ignited and burnt with the evolution of gases. The resulting gel was left for continuous heating until the completion of the reaction was achieved by self-propagated process. The compound was combusted at 150 °C which was completed in 30 min. A foamy and highly porous product so obtained was ground and annealed in air at 950 °C for 8 h in a PID-controlled box furnace where the heating and cooling rates were maintained at 20 °C/min. The final powder was ground in pestle and mortar to form a fine powder for further characterization (Scheme 1). The following stoichiometric ratios were employed for the preparation of ferrites precursor: Ba(NO3)2 + x[Co(NO3)2 .6H2O] + x[ZrO(NO3)2 ] + 12 − 2x[Fe(NO3)3 .9H2O] Urea −−−−−−−−−−→ BaCoxZrxFe12−2xO19 Where (x = 0.0, 0.2 0.4.0.6, 0.8, and 1.0)
Journal: Journal of Superconductivity and Novel Magnetism

Synthesis_Procedure: Polycrystalline hexaferrites with composition BaFe12-2xCuxTixO19 (x = 0, 1, 1.5, 2) were synthesized by the ceramic technique using high purity Fe2O3 (Sigma-Aldrich), CuO, BaO and TiO2 (all Merck). These oxides were mixed in proper stoichiometry; ground in acetone (Merck) for 6 h and presintered at 900°C for 12 h. For BaM, Dho et al. [16] reported that, as the sintering temperature increases from 1100°C to 1300°C, large grains with dimensions of a few microns and better intergrain connectivity are obtained. Therefore, the final sintering temperature of the ferrite x = 0 was 1300°C. In our earlier publication [17] with Mg–Ti substituted in BaM, the sintering temperature was 1300°C for all the compositions of Mg–Ti, but here due to the low melting point of CuO (1360°C), the solid solution of the ferrites, x = 1, 1.5, 2 melted even when the sintering temperature was reduced to 1200°C. Therefore the samples x = 1, 1.5 and 2 were finally sintered at1100°C for 24 h. These sintered samples were finely crushed and pressed into pellets of 10 mm diameter; and sintered at the final respective sintering temperatures. The cooling rate was 4°C/min throughout; up to room temperature. The sintering was carried out in electronically controlled furnace.

Ti-Co co-substituted M-type barium ferrite Ba(TiCo)xFe12-2xO19 particles were prepared by the citrate precursor method with the initial Ba:Fe=1:10.8. The raw materials include Fe(NO3)3·9H2O, Ba(NO3)2, Co(NO3)2·6H2O, tetra-n-butyl titanate and citric acid. The aqueous solution and ethyl alcohol solution of the cations and citric acid were prepared separately. Then the solutions of the cations were successively stirred into the prepared citric acid solution drop by drop. Next a certain amount of ammonia solution was added into the solution to change the pH value to 7.The mixture was evaporated at 70 ºC for hours until the liquid mixture became dark brown gel and the gel was dried in vacuum oven. Finally, it was decomposed at a temperature of 450 ºC for 4h and annealed at the temperature of 950ºC for 4h in the muffle furnace.

The schematic of the synthesis process was illustrated in Fig. 1. The reagents used in the experiment were listed in Table 1. A certain amount of Sr(NO)2 and Fe(NO3)3·9H2O were dissolved in 50 ml of deionized water. Then citric acid was added to the above mixture (weighed by a molar ratio of citric acid to metal ions of 1:1) and stirred well, adjusting the pH to 7 and the water bath temperature to 70 °C. Subsequently, the solution was heated and stirred in a constanttemperature magnetic agitator until it became soluble, and then dried at 250 °C for 3 h to obtain the gel [31]. The gel was ground into a fine powder and calcined at 800 °C, 900 °C, 1000 °C, and 1100 °C for 3 h in a chamber resistance furnace. The samples were recorded as SFO-800, SFO-900, SFO1000, and SFO-1100, respectively. The Sr1 − xPrxFe12O19 (0 ≤ x ≤ 0.1) and Sr0.95Re0.05Fe12O19 (Re = La, Pr, Nd, Dy, Yb) samples followed the same procedure with a calcination temperature of 900 °C. The Sr1 − xPrxFe12O19 samples were recorded as SPFO-0, SPFO-0.025, SPFO-0.05, SPFO-0.075 and SPFO-0.1 with x = 0, 0.025, 0.05, 0.075 and 0.1, respectively. The Sr0.95Re0.05Fe12O19 samples were recorded as SLFO-0.05, SPFO-0.05, SNFO-0.05, SDFO-0.05, SYFO0.05, with Re = La, Pr, Nd, Dy, and Yb, respectively.

All the chemicals, Strontium carbonate (SrCO3, Alfa Aesar, ≥99%) Iron (III) nitrate nonahydrate (Fe(NO3)3⋅9H2O, Sigma Aldrich, ≥99.9%), Acetic acid, (CH3COOH, Merck, 100%), Citric acid (C6H8O7, Merck, ≥99.5%), Ammonia solution (NH3, Merck, 25%) and Neodymium nitrate (Nd(NO3)3⋅6H2O, Sigma Aldrich, ≥99.8%) were AR/GR grade Product. All the materials were used without any purification. The neodymium doped strontium hexaferrite was synthesized by the auto combustion route. The stoichiometric amount of neodymium nitrate (Nd(NO3)3⋅6H2O) and iron nitrate (Fe(NO3)3⋅6H2O) were dissolved in the minimum amount of de-ionized water to form solutions I, II respectively. Another solution (III) was prepared by dissolving strontium carbonate (SrCO3) into the minimum amount of acetic acid (CH3COOH). The above solutions (I, II, III) were mixed to form a solution IV. Further, a solution (V) was made by dissolving citric acid (C6H8O7) into de-ionized water. The citric acid was taken in 1: 1 M ratio of metal ions. Finally, the solution IV and V were mixed to form a resulting solution. The pH of the resulting solution was kept at 7 by adding ammonia solution. The resulting solution was heated continuously at 80°C with stirring at 200 rpm until the solution converted into wet gel. On further heating, the wet gel undergone self ignition reaction and formed a low density powder having temple like structure. The detailed experimental procedure is shown in Fig. 1. The developed material was grounded to form fine powder which finally casted into the rectangular pallets.

In order to synthesize strontium hexaferrite via sol-gel auto-combustion method, we use strontium nitrate Sr(NO3)2 (Sigma Aldrich, ≥98%), Ferric nitrate nonahydrate Fe(NO3)3,9H2O (Sigma Aldrich, ≥98%), citric acid (Solvachim, 99.5%) and ammonia solution (Sigma Aldrich, 25% NH3 basis). Distilled water was used to prepare the solutions. Stoichiometric amounts of these precursors were dissolved in distilled water by magnetic stirring. In order to obtain around neutral pH-value [14], ammonia was added to the obtained solution. The solution was then dried at 100 °C so that we obtain a gel which is heated until auto-combustion takes place. The obtained as-synthesized powder was then calcined at 800, 1000 and 1100 °C.

All samples of M-type hexagonal ferrites Sr1−xCoxNdxFe12−xO19 (x = 0, 0.08, 0.16, and 0.24) were synthesized by the ball-milling-assisted ceramic process.27 The starting materials used in this study were SrC2O4·H2O, FeC2O4·2H2O, Nd2(C2O4)3·10H2O, and CoC2O4·2H2O of analytical grade. First, mixtures of the starting materials were milled in a stainless steel ball-milling tank of 100 ml for 30 min with an angular velocity of 350 rpm, and a ball-to-powder weight ratio of about 15:1; then, the mixed powder was dried at 80°C in air for 5 h. Finally, the mixed powder was calcined at 950°C, 1050°C, and 1150°C for 2.5 h, respectively, at a heating rate of 2°C min−1 in air to produce M-type hexagonal Sr1−xCoxNdxFe12−xO19.

Starting materials of SrCO3 (98.0 wt%), Fe2O3 (99.0 wt%), La2O3 (99.99 wt%), and Co2O3 (99.0 wt%) powders were weighed in the composition of Sr0.7La0.3Fe11.7Co0.3O19 for preparing the La3 + –Co2 + substituted ferrites. The mixed powders were calcinated at 1250 °C for 2 h and then ball-milled with 2–5 wt% BBSZ glass at 400 r/min for 4 h to get powders with average particle size about 1.1–1.2 μm. Powders with 6 wt% polyvinyl alcohol (PVA) binder were pressed into disks with a diameter of 12 mm at 45 MPa, and then sintered at 850 °C by CS method for 2 h, MS method for 30 min, and HPS method for 30 min, respectively. Work frequency and output power of the microwave sintering furnace (GER-M2) is 2.45 GHz and 2000 W. Maximal sintering temperature and pressure of the customized hot press sintering system can arrive at 1000 °C and 60 MPa.

Synthesis_Procedure: Here, SrFe12−xNbxO19 ceramics, with x = 0.00 and 0.03 (abbreviated as SFO and SFN3O), were prepared by the conventional solid-state method using raw materials of SrCO3 (purity ≥ 99.9%, Aldrich), Nb2O5 (purity ≥ 99.9%, Alfa Aesar), and Fe2O3 (purity ≥ 99.945%, Alfa Aesar). The chemicals were preheated at 200 °C for 24 h and then weighed according to the stoichiometric formula. They were ball milled in ethanol for 12 h at 250 rpm using stainless balls and vessels. The slurry was dried, and the powder product was calcined at 1100 °C for 6 h. To reduce the particle size, the calcined powder was ball milled again. The fine precursor was mixed with 5 wt % PVA and then pressed into pellets with a diameter of 13 mm and thickness of 1−2 mm. The pellets were heated at 800 °C for 2 h in air to remove the binder. Sintering was carried out at 1200 °C for 6 h in air. The sintered pellets were polished and then annealed in air for 12 h at 1000 °C.

Polycrystalline M-type barium hexaferrite BaFe12O19 (BFO) and scandium doped barium hexaferrites (BaFe12-xScxO19) with the doping concentrations x = 1.5 and 2.5 (BaFe10.5Sc1.5O19 and BaFe9.5Sc2.5O19) were prepared by conventional solid state route. Synthesis_Procedure: Analytical grade chemical reagents (purity 99.99%, Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO, USA) strontium nitrate (SrNO3)2), iron (III) nitrate nonahydrate (FeNO3)3.9H2O, calcium nitrate tetrahydrate (Ca NO 3 ) 3 .6H2O), scandium (III) nitrate nonahydrate ((ScNO3)3.9H2O), and citric acid were used for the synthesis of Sr1-x/12Cax/12Fe12-xScxO19 (x = 0.0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0, 1.25, 1.5, and 2.0) compounds. Table 1 lists the stoichiometric composition of nitrate salt used for the synthesis of compounds. The sol-gel autocombustion technique was adapted for the synthesis of compounds. These chemicals’ stoichiometric ratio was dissolved in water and sonicated for 30 min in the autocombustion process. Then ammonium hydroxide (30.0% NH3 basis) solution was added dropwise to the clear solution. After regulating the pH at 6.5, the solution was heated on a hot plate at 150oC until it became a highly viscous gel, and after that, the temperature was increased to 250oC. The gel then started to burn and formed a voluminous material. Thus, obtained powder was crushed in the mortar and annealed at 1100oC for 12 h in a box furnace in air.

These chemicals’ stoichiometric ratio was dissolved in water and sonicated for 30 min in the autocombustion process. Then ammonium hydroxide (30.0% NH3 basis) solution was added dropwise to the clear solution. After regulating the pH at 6.5, the solution was heated on a hot plate at 150oC until it became a highly viscous gel, and after that, the temperature was increased to 250oC. The gel then started to burn and formed a voluminous material. Thus, obtained powder was crushed in the mortar and annealed at 1100oC for 12 h in a box furnace in air.
Journal: Journal of Superconductivity and Novel Magnetism

Synthesis_Procedure: Microcrystalline samples of strontium M-type hexaferrite SrFe12-xInxO19 (with doping levels x = 1.7, 1.8 and 2.0 Indium atoms per formula unit (f.u.)) were synthesized via the citrate gel combustion method using nitrates Sr(NO3)2, Fe(NO3)3⋅9H2O, In(NO3)3⋅3H2O, (NH4)OH and C6H8O7 (all Sigma-Aldrich, technical grade, purity >98 %) as precursors. The as-synthesized powders were subsequently annealed at 1200 °C for 1 h in an air atmosphere. For nanoparticle production the SrFe12-xInxO19 microcrystalline powders were subjected to high-energy ball milling using a planetary ball mill PM 400 (Retsch, Germany) at a rotational speed of 400 rpm for 50 h. The milling medium comprised 1-octadecene with oleic acid (OA) added as a surfactant. A powder-to-ball mass ratio of 1:10 was maintained. Following milling, the particles were washed to remove residual 1-octadecene and transferred into dichloromethane (DCM). Ultrasonic homogenization was then performed to disrupt particle agglomerates. Subsequently, the particles were coated with hydrophilic biocompatible Pluronic F-127 copolymer to enable aqueous stabilization. For coating, powder suspensions were prepared in toluene. An aqueous solution of Pluronic F-127 was then introduced to the toluene suspensions. An emulsion was formed via ultrasonic homogenization. This emulsion was centrifuged, resulting in phase separation where the toluene migrated to form the upper phase. The toluene phase was carefully decanted and replaced with deionized water with subsequent sonication until a homogeneous sol is formed. After that the final hydrophilized nanoparticles were collected by centrifugation.

High purity (99.9%) Fe(NO3)3·9H2O, BaCO3, IrCl4, ZnCl2, CoCO3 · xH2O and La(NO3)3·6H2O were used as the starting materials for sample preparation; the Fe/ Ba ratio of 11.6 was used. The procedure to obtain BaMIr–Co powders was as follows. The sols were prepared by dissolving Fe(NO3)3·9H2O and IrCl4 into deionised water in the desired amounts. Precipitation of iron and iridium hydroxides was carried out with a concentrated ammonia solution. The precipitate was filtered and washed to eliminate the (NO3)−1 and Cl−1 anions. Then, this was dissolved into a vigorously stirred citric acid solution at 60°C. At this stage, BaCO3 and CoCO3 · xH2O, were added to achieve the desired composition. A small amount of ethylene glycol and benzoic acid were also introduced into the solution to act as second co-ordinating agents. To prepare BaMLa–Zn powders we proceeded in the same way as for BaMIr–Co, however, the Zn2+ and La3+ sources being also dissolved in the first stage. The gels were obtained by slowly evaporating solution at 90°C for several hours and then heating at 140°C. Then the gels were pre-heated at 450°C for 5 h to eliminate the organic compounds. Finally, the obtained powders were annealed at 975°C for 2 h to synthesise samples with magnetoplumbite structure.
Journal: Journal of Magnetism and Magnetic Materials

Synthesis_Procedure: Analytical grade of Ba(NO3)2 , Fe(NO3)3·9H2O, Zn(NO3)2·6H2O, NbCl5, and D-fructose are used as raw materials. The chemicals are weighed and mixed according to determined proportion. Nitrates, choloride, and D-fructose solutions are mixed with continuous stirring and heated up to 80 °C to get a sticky liquid gel. Then the mixture is heated at 130 °C in a hot air oven for 2 days, which turns it into a dried precursor. Powders of the dried precursor are calcined. The calcined powder is uniaxilly pressed into pellets using a hydraulic press using polyvinyl alcohol (PVA) as a binder.
Journal: Journal of Superconductivity and Novel Magnetism

Synthesis_Procedure: The samples of strontium hexaferrite series having definite composition Sr1−xDyxFe12−yCoyO19 (where x = 0.00–0.15; y = 0.00–0.60) were synthesized by sol–gel combustion method. Following precursors were used: ferric nitrate nona-hydrate Fe(NO3)3∙9H2O (Aldrich, 99.9%), strontium nitrate hexahydrate Sr(NO3)2∙6H2O (Fluka ≥ 99%), dysprosium nitrate pentahydrate Dy(NO3)3∙5H2O (Aldrich, 99.9%), cobalt nitrate tetrahydrate Co(NO3)2.4H2O (Merck, 99%), ammonia solution (Riedel, 33%) and ethylene glycol (Riedel–Dehaen, > 99.5%). Stoichiometric compositions were prepared by mixing together aqueous solutions of metallic nitrates and ethylene glycol under constant stirring at room temperature. The ratio of metal nitrates and ethylene glycol was taken as 1:1. The pH of the solution was adjusted at 7.0 by adding 2M ammonia solution drop wise. The mixture was heated at 90 °C till a brown color gel was obtained. The as obtained gel was heated till combustion, ultimately leaving behind loose ashes. The whole powder was then annealed in temperature programmed muffle furnace (VULCANTM A550) at 950 °C for 5 h.

Synthesis_Procedure: Analytical-grade ferric chloride (FeCl3·6H2O), strontium chloride (SrCl2·6H2O), nickel chloride (NiCl2·6H2O), lanthanum chloride (LaCl3·7H2O), and NaOH were used to produce Sr0.8La0.2NixFe12−xO19 nanoparticles by a coprecipitation method.22 Stoichiometric amounts of strontium chloride and lanthanum chloride were dissolved completely in ultrapure deionized water to make aqueous solution I. Ferric chloride and nickel chloride were also mixed in ultrapure deionized water to make aqueous solution II. Sufficient NaOH was dissolved completely in ultrapure deionized water to make aqueous solution III with molarity of 0.7 M. To determine the optimal solution conditions for single-phase formation, three types of aqueous solutions were then produced at different molarity and pH values. In the first type, solutions I and II were mixed in 0.1:0.5 molar ratio and added to solution III at volume ratio of (III)/(I + II) ≈ 2.6 at 80°C and reaction pH of 7. In the second type, solutions I and II were mixed at 0.1:1 molar ratio and added to solution III again at volume ratio of (III)/(I + II) ≈ 2.6 at 80°C and reaction pH of 7. In the third type, solutions I and II were mixed at 0.1:1 molar ratio and added to solution III at volume ratio of (III)/(I + II) ≈ 5.2 at 80°C and reaction pH of about 13. A series of samples with Ni content from 0.2 to 1 in steps of 0.2 were then fabricated at the optimal conditions. Aqueous suspensions of all samples were stirred gently for 2 h to achieve chemical homogeneity. Brownish ferrite particles precipitated from this mixture and were washed with pure water to remove NaCl and NaOH, then dried at 100°C in air atmosphere overnight. All of the precipitated nanocrystalline powders were calcined at 1200°C for 6 h in air atmosphere.

M-type hexaferrites were synthesized via a solid-state reaction method with nominal compositions of SrFe12 − 2xAlxCrxO19 (x = 0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3), SrFe11.5M0.1Al0.2Cr0.2O19 (M = Mn, Co), and Sr0.9R0.1Fe11.6Al0.2Cr0.2O19 (R = La, Ce). The precursor and sintering additive powders used for phase formation included SrCO3, CaCO3, Cr2O3, MnCO3, and Co3O4 (all ≥ 99.9% purity, Kojundo Chemical Lab. Co., Ltd.), Fe2O3 (~ 99.5%, industrial grade, Korea), and SiO2 (99.0%, industrial grade, China). These were weighed according to the molar ratios of each chemical composition. The powder mixtures were placed in polypropylene bottles along with yttria-stabilized ZrO2 balls and deionized water (DI water), and subjected to ball milling at a rotational speed of 100 rpm for 24 h. The mixed powders were dried in an oven of 120 °C, placed in an alumina crucible, and calcined in an air atmosphere furnace at 1100 °C for 4 h. The calcined powders were then pulverized, sieved, and subjected to a second round of ball milling at a rotational speed of 120 rpm for 20 h. In the second milling stage, SiO2 along with either CaCO3 or SrCO3 was added as sintering additives. The powders obtained after secondary ball milling were dried in the oven, placed into circular molds with a diameter of 20.0 mm, and pressed into pellets using a pressure of approximately 9.4 MPa. The fabricated pellets were subsequently sintered in air at temperatures ranging from 1210 °C to 1250 °C for 2 h.

In the present work, the samples weighing 10 g were prepared by mechanical alloying from the raw powders of Fe2O3 (99% purity) and SrCO3 (>97%), and they were mixed together in order to obtain a Sr/Fe ratio of 1 : 12. The milling processes were performed either in high-energy mill using 10 mm hardened steel balls, or in centrifugal planetary ball mill using three sizes of steel balls with diameters of 8, 10 or 12 mm. For the first sort of milling process using 10 mm balls in a high-energy mill, an angular velocity of 400 rpm and a ball to powder weight ratio of 7.5 : 1 were chosen. For other milling processes, a velocity of 125 rpm and two powder weight ratios of 15 : 1 and 7.5 : 1 were selected. Some as-milled samples were pressed at room temperature into rectangular specimens having a size of 4 × 1 × 0.5 cm 3. The calculated densities after pressing were about 4.0 g/cm 3, and similar to those of samples prepared by Ding et al. [8]. Both milling and pressing were performed in air. Most of the specimens obtained were annealed at different temperatures for a fixed time of 1 h. In addition, in order to study the detailed influence of annealing time on magnetic properties, one special kind of as-milled powder was chosen for heat treatment at 1000°C for a different time. Finally, the samples were rapidly quenched in air or cooled in the furnace for comparing the effect of the cooling condition on properties.
Journal: Journal of Magnetism and Magnetic Materials
Synthesis_Notes: planetary mill, 10 mm balls, ball/powder 15:1, 125 rpm

Synthesis_Procedure: Fifteen hexaferrite samples with the general composition BaFe12−x−y MgxZryO19 (MgZr(1)–MgZr(15)) were synthesized using sodium carbonate as a flux, with nominal substitution levels of xnom = ynom = 0.10–1.50 in increments of 0.10. Appropriate molar amounts of BaCO3 (p.a., Carl Roth, Karlsruhe, Germany), Fe2O3 (99.0%, Riedel de Haën, Seelze, Germany), MgO (p.a., Merck, Darmstadt, Germany), ZrO2 (PSZ, Merck), and 25 mol-% Na2CO3 (p.a., Honeywell, Charlotte, NC, USA) were thoroughly mixed, ground in an agate mortar, and heated in a platinum crucible under air to 1300 °C over a period of ten hours. This temperature was maintained for 36 h, followed by cooling to 500 °C for 60 h. The furnace was then switched off, and the resulting crude product was washed with halfconcentrated nitric acid and demineralized water. The obtained products never contained any remains of carbonates, but occasionally minor amounts of platinum from mechanical separation from the crucible surface, according to powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD). In the case of single-phase products, synthesis and post-treatment typically yielded more than 90% of the expected amount of product. For information on by-products of highly substituted samples close or above the maximal degree of substitution, please refer to the individual sections in the manuscript, particularly Section 3.1 (PXRD and lattice parameters). The BaFe12−x−yMgxHfyO19 series includes eight samples (MgHf(1)–MgHf(8)) with xnom = ynom = 0.20–1.60 (0.20 increments). Hafnium was introduced using HfO2 (99.9%, Zr ≤ 0.5%, Merck). The synthesis followed the same procedure as for the Mg/Zr-substituted materials. Additionally, an unsubstituted BaFe12O19 (BaM) sample was prepared as a reference.

The chemicals used for the synthesis of the samples were Fe(NO3)3.9H2O (97% Riedel de Haen), CaCl2.2H2O (99% Merck), Sr(NO3)2 (99%Fluka), TaCl5 (99% Aldrich), KCl (99% Merck) and ammonia solution (33% Merck). Solutions of all metal salts were prepared in deionized water except tantalum chloride. Tantalum chloride was not soluble in deionized water. That's why the required amount of this salt was initially dissolved in small amount of aqua regia (3HCl and HNO3) on a hot plate with magnetic stirrer. Then this dissolved salt solution was transferred into the measuring flask and made the volume of this solution up to the mark by adding the deionized water in it. Tantalum and potassium substituted M-type Sr–Ca hexaferrites with nominal composition Sr0.5Ca0.5Fe12-2xTaxKxO19 (x = 0.0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4) have been prepared by the sol gel combustion procedure. In this method, solutions of all metal salts in equal volumes were mixed in a 2000 ml beaker. To this mixture 250 ml of 0.195 M citric acid solution was added as chelating agent. The molar ratio of citric acid to total moles of metal ions was adjusted as 1:1.5. The solutions of all the metal salts and chelating agent were homogenized on a hot plate with magnetic stirrer. The mixed solution was then neutralized to pH 7 by dropwise addition of 4.0 M ammonia solution. The evaporation of neutralized solution was done by heating it at 300–353 K on a hot plate with continuous stirring, until it became a viscous gel. Increasing the temperature upto 673 K led to ignition of the gel. Finally, ash burnt powders were annealed in air at the temperature of 1223 K for 6 h in a furnace (VULCAN™ A-550) to attain the magnetoplumbite phase in the synthesized hexaferrite.

That's why the required amount of this salt was initially dissolved in small amount of aqua regia (3HCl and HNO3) on a hot plate with magnetic stirrer. Then this dissolved salt solution was transferred into the measuring flask and made the volume of this solution up to the mark by adding the deionized water in it. Tantalum and potassium substituted M-type Sr–Ca hexaferrites with nominal composition Sr0.5Ca0.5Fe12-2xTaxKxO19 (x = 0.0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4) have been prepared by the sol gel combustion procedure. In this method, solutions of all metal salts in equal volumes were mixed in a 2000 ml beaker. To this mixture 250 ml of 0.195 M citric acid solution was added as chelating agent. The molar ratio of citric acid to total moles of metal ions was adjusted as 1:1.5. The solutions of all the metal salts and chelating agent were homogenized on a hot plate with magnetic stirrer. The mixed solution was then neutralized to pH 7 by dropwise addition of 4.0 M ammonia solution. The evaporation of neutralized solution was done by heating it at 300–353 K on a hot plate with continuous stirring, until it became a viscous gel. Increasing the temperature upto 673 K led to ignition of the gel. Finally, ash burnt powders were annealed in air at the temperature of 1223 K for 6 h in a furnace (VULCAN™ A-550) to attain the magnetoplumbite phase in the synthesized hexaferrite.

SrFe12-2xCux/2Cox/2TixO19 (named as CCT-SrM, x = 0, 0.05, 0.10, and 0.15) samples were prepared by using the solid-state reaction method. SrCO3, Fe2O3, CuO, Co3O4, and TiO2 with purities above 99.9% purchased from Sigma-Aldrich were used as precursors. Precursors with the appropriate amounts were mixed in 1 h using a Retsch MM200 miller. Then, the powders were pressed into a button shape and annealed at 1000 °C for 10 h. After annealing, the samples were crushed and remilled for 1 h followed by sintering at 1000 °C for 12 h to get the final products.

A series of Mg–Zr substituted Ba(MgZr)xFe12− 2xO19 (with x=0.0, 0.3, 0.6 and 1.0) precursor pellets has been prepared by a conventional solid state reaction method. High purity BaCO3, Fe2O3, MgO, and ZrO2 chemicals were mixed in desired stoichiometric amount and ball milled for 24 h. The ball milled powder was then calcined at 1000 °C for 10 h. After adding 2 wt% aqueous solution of polyvinyl alcohol to the calcined powder, it was subjected to hand grinding for 1 h and then pelletized. The pellets were subjected to two different processing techniques: (1) conventional sintering in furnace at 1200 °C for 5 h, and (2) microwave processing in H-field in a single mode cylindrical cavity (in TE011 mode) either at 1100 °C for 10 min, in each case, or at 1200 °C for 5 min at microwave frequency of 2.45 GHz. The sample temperature was measured by an optical pyrometer (Raytek, RAYMA2SCSF).

Hexaferrites with chemical formula SrCoxZrxFe12−2xO19 (noted SrCoZr hereafter) and SrNixZrxFe12−2xO19 (noted SrNiZr hereafter) where x ≤ 0.1 were produced using a sonochemical assisted route. All the chemicals used are of analytical and received from sigma Aldrich. Stoichiometric amounts of strontium nitrate (99%), cobalt nitrate hexahydrate (99%), nickel(II) nitrate hexahydrate (99%), zirconium oxynitrate (99%) and iron (III) nitrate nonahydrate (98%), all are analytical grade (sigma Aldrich) were dissolved in 80 ml of deionized H2O with vigorous stirring. The pH was regulated at 11 with the help of a NaOH solution. The mixture was then exposed to ultrasonic irradiation with 20 kHz frequency and 70 W power, Ultrasonic homogenizer UZ SONOPULS HD 2070) for 30 min. The obtained powder was washed many times with deionized H2O and dried at 80 °C. Finally, the powdered products were calcinated at 1050 °C for 4 h.
Journal: Journal of Magnetism and Magnetic Materials

Stoichiometric amounts of strontium nitrate (99%), cobalt nitrate hexahydrate (99%), nickel(II) nitrate hexahydrate (99%), zirconium oxynitrate (99%) and iron (III) nitrate nonahydrate (98%), all are analytical grade (sigma Aldrich) were dissolved in 80 ml of deionized H2O with vigorous stirring. The pH was regulated at 11 with the help of a NaOH solution. The mixture was then exposed to ultrasonic irradiation with 20 kHz frequency and 70 W power, Ultrasonic homogenizer UZ SONOPULS HD 2070) for 30 min. The obtained powder was washed many times with deionized H2O and dried at 80 °C. Finally, the powdered products were calcinated at 1050 °C for 4 h.

Synthesis_Procedure: SrFe12-xAlxO19 (x = 0, 1, 1.4, 2, 2.4) were prepared by sol–gel combustion from Fe(NO3)3⋅9H2O, Al(NO3)3⋅9H2O, and Sr(NO3)2 as metal precursors. The molar ratio of total trivalent cations to strontium was fixed at (Fe3++Al3+)/Sr2+ = 11. This value, slightly lower than the stoichiometric ratio of 12 for SrFe12O19, was chosen to introduce a small excess of Sr2+ in the reaction mixture to compensate for possible Sr volatilization during the combustion and calcination steps and to favor single-phase formation. After gelation (citric acid, pH=7), the dried gel was combusted at 300 °C, ground, and annealed at 1100 °C for 6 h in air. This series is referred to as SFAO_x and SFO, respectively. More info on the synthesis is reported in Ref [24].

SrFe12−2x (Mg,Co)x/2TixO19 nanoparticles with different x (x = 0.0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2 and 2.5) were prepared by a co-precipitation method. The stoichiometric amount of chloride compounds of Sr, Fe, Mg, Co and Ti with chemical compositions of SrCl2·6H2O, FeCl3·6H2O, MgCl2·6H2O, CoCl2·6H2O and TiCl4 were dissolved in deionized water at 70 °C to form a homogeneous solution. Then the pH of the solution was adjusted slowly to 13 by adding drop wise alkaline sodium hydroxide (NaOH 1 M) solution to form a brownish yellow suspension of the hybrid complex. The resulted gel was washed with deionized water for several time and then filtered and dried at 100 °C and then calcined at 900 °C for 1 h.

Barium Nitrate (Ba(NO3)2, SDFCL, 99.5% purity), Strontium Nitrate (Sr(NO3)2, SDFCL, 99.0% purity), Cobalt Nitrate (Co(NO3)2.6H2O, EMPLURA, ≥ 98.0%), Calcium Nitrate (Ca(No3)2, BURGOYNE, 98% purity), Ferric Nitrate (Fe(NO3)3•9H2O, HPLC, > 99.0% purity), Citric Acid (C6H8O7•H2O, HPLC, 99.5%) and ammonia solution (25% w/v, HPLC) were used as starting materials. The polycrystalline Ba0.25Sr0.75CoxCaxFe12-2xO19 hexaferrite samples were prepared using a sol-gel auto combustion technique. High purity of Ba (NO3)2, Sr (NO3)2, Co (NO3)2.6H2O, Ca (NO3)2, Fe (NO3)3•9H2O and citric acid were used as raw materials to prepare Ba0.25Sr0.75CoxCaxFe12-2xO19 (x = 0.0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.8, 1.2, 1.6 and 2.0) hexaferrites. Stoichiometric proportions of these metal nitrates were first dissolved into deionised water to form metal nitrate solution. Then citric acid was added dropwise in 1:1 M ratio in the prepared metal nitrate solution. The mixture was kept on a magnetic stirrer under continuous stirring of 30 min and, the pH of the mixed solution was adjusted to 7 by adding the ammonia solution (25% w/v). The solution was heated at 80 °C and after sometime, it was converted into a viscous gel. After further heating, ignitions started and the dried gel burnt in self-propagating combustion and forming ash-like powder. Finally, the as-burnt powder was preheated at 550 °C for 4 h followed by final heating of 1150 °C for 5 h in a muffle furnace. The material was then slowly cooled to room temperature to obtain Ba0.25Sr0.75CoxCaxFe12-2xO19 hexaferrite powder. A flowchart for preparing Ba0.25Sr0.75CoxCaxFe12-2xO19 hexaferrite powder is shown in Fig. 1.

The experimental procedure for synthesizing Co–Ti doped BaM ferrite nano powders consisted of two steps including chemical coprecipitation and secondary heating treatment by molten salts, which was described as: 1) Chemical co-precipitation process: an aqueous solution containing Ba2+, Fe3+, Co2+ and Ti4+ in the molar ratio according to chemical formula of BaCoxTixFe12-2xO19 was firstly prepared with the concentration of Fe3+ of 0.5 mol/L. Iron nitrate nonahydrate (Fe (NO3)3⋅9H2O), barium chloride dihydrate (BaCl2⋅2H2O), cobaltous nitrate hexahydrate (Co(NO3)2⋅6H2O), and titanic chloride-hydrochloric acid solution (with both concentrations of TiCl4 and HCl of 3 mol/L) were used as starting materials. Sodium hydroxide (NaOH) and sodium carbonate (Na2CO3) mixed solution was employed as the precipitator and added dropwise into the aqueous solution under continuous stirring. The molar amount of NaOH was 20% in excess of the total metal ions expect of Ba2+, while the molar amount of Na2CO3 was 50% in excess of Ba2+. A suspension formed subsequently. After filtering, washing and drying operations, the precipitated precursor powders were obtained. 2) Heating treatment by molten salts: Sodium chloride (NaCl) and potassium chloride (KCl) were used as the molten salts with their weight ratio of 1:1. The precursor powders were mixed with the molten salts with the weight ratio of 1:2 and the mixture was calcined at 900 °C for 2 h. After washing the calcined powders by hot water for several time to eliminate the molten salts, the targeted ferrite nano powders were obtained.

Sodium hydroxide (NaOH) and sodium carbonate (Na2CO3) mixed solution was employed as the precipitator and added dropwise into the aqueous solution under continuous stirring. The molar amount of NaOH was 20% in excess of the total metal ions expect of Ba2+, while the molar amount of Na2CO3 was 50% in excess of Ba2+. A suspension formed subsequently. After filtering, washing and drying operations, the precipitated precursor powders were obtained. 2) Heating treatment by molten salts: Sodium chloride (NaCl) and potassium chloride (KCl) were used as the molten salts with their weight ratio of 1:1. The precursor powders were mixed with the molten salts with the weight ratio of 1:2 and the mixture was calcined at 900 °C for 2 h. After washing the calcined powders by hot water for several time to eliminate the molten salts, the targeted ferrite nano powders were obtained.

A series of M-type hexaferrites of compositions Ba0.25Sr0.75PrxFe12− xO19 (x=0.00, 0.05, 0.10, 0.15, 0.20, 0.25) were synthesized using sol–gel auto-combustion method. Aqueous solutions of Sr(NO3)2 (99%, Sigma Aldrich), FeCl3 (98%, Sigma Aldrich ) and Ba(NO3)2 (99.8%, Sigma Aldrich) were prepared in deionized water according to stoichiometric calculations. Stirring of these solutions was done for 3 h without heating. During this process citric acid were slowly added. The molar ratio of metal nitrates to citric acid was kept as 1:1. The calculated amount of Pr2O3 for each sample was dissolved in nitric acid (concentrated) and heated at low temperature (80 °C) to make its nitrate and then added to the solution. The resultant solution was then stirred on magnetic stirrer and heated at a temperature of 80 °C. The pH value of the solution was adjusted to 7–8 by adding ammonia solution (ammonia/water=40/60) in the prepared solution. At this temperature deionized water starts evaporating for about 5 h and reaction was started after complete evaporation. At the end greenish gel is formed which is further heated and this gel transferred to powdered sample by auto-combustion. The powder was then properly grinded in an agate mortar and pestle. This grinded powder was then pressed into pellets (with dimensions of 7 mm diameter and about 2 mm thickness) at a pressure of ~ 40 kN for about 1–2 min using Paul-Otto Weber hydraulic press. The pellets and powdered samples were heat treated simultaneously at a temperature of 800 °C for 3 h and then finally sintered at 1200 °C for 1 h at the rate of 10 °C/min to obtain M-type hexaferrites. The samples were furnace cooled by lowering the temperature at the same rate to obtain the equilibrium position of the cations.

Synthesis_Procedure: Powder samples of Sr1-xYxFe12O19 (x = 0, 0.05, 0.1, 0.15) were prepared via the sol-gel method. The raw materials used were strontium nitrate (Sr(NO3)2), iron nitrate nonahydrate (Fe(NO3)3⋅9H2O), and yttrium nitrate hexahydrate (Y(NO3)3⋅6H2O), all of analytical purity and requiring no further purification. First, the raw materials were dissolved in deionized water according to the stoichiometric ratio. Citric acid was then added at a ratio of metal ions to citric acid of 1:1.5, and the pH was adjusted to ~7 with ammonia solution. The mixed solution was heated at 80 °C with stirring until a dry gel formed. The obtained gel was dried at 150 °C for 5 h and then thoroughly ground to obtain dry gel powder. To remove residual nitrides and carbides from the powder, it was preheated in a muffle furnace at 600 °C for 3 h followed by regrinding. Finally, the powder was placed in a muffle furnace at 1200 °C for 4 h and allowed to cool naturally to obtain powder samples with varying Y3+doping levels.

High purity materials, Fe (NO3)3 . 9H2O (Merck, >99%), Sr (NO3)2 (Merck, >99%), SnCl4 (Merck, >99%), Mg (C2H3O2)2 .4H2O (Merck, >99.5%) and NaOH (Merck, >99%) were used in the synthesis of samples. Initially iron nitrate and strontium nitrate with Fe3+ /Sr2+ molar ratio of 9 were dissolved in a mixture of deionized water/ethanol (50/50) as the solvent. Then tin chloride and magnesium acetate were added to the solvent to achieve stoichiometry of SrFe12−x (Sn0.5Mg0.5)xO19 where x = 0.0–1.0. The hexaferrite precursors were precipitated by addition of NaOH solution (2 M) as a precipitating agent at pH 13. After drying at 80 °C, the precipitates were calcined at 700 and 800 °C for 2 h.

Two samples of hexaferrite nanoplatelets, unsubstituted BHF nanoplatelets and Sc-substituted Sc-BHF nanoplatelets, were synthesized using the hydrothermal method. A total of 200 mL of aqueous solution of metal nitrates (20.8 mmol/L Ba2+, Ba2+/ (Fe3++Sc3+) = 1/5, for Sc-BHF Fe3+/Sc3+ = 7, the used materials are listed in Supporting information) was rapidly mixed into 200 mL of aqueous NaOH (4.65 mol/L) to co-precipitate the corresponding hydroxides. The slurry was then sealed in an Inconel pressure vessel (Parr Instrument Company) and heated at a rate of 3 °C/min to the final temperature, when the heating was switched-off. Because of the relatively large thermal capacity, the temperature inside the autoclave started to decrease after approximately 10 min. Since the addition of Sc3+ effectively suppresses the exaggerated growth during the hydrothermal synthesis of the nanoplatelets [7,8], the two samples were synthesized at different temperatures. The aim was to synthesize nanoplatelets of comparable size. The unsubstituted BHF sample was synthesized at 160 °C and the Scsubstituted Sc-BHF sample at 250 °C. The product was washed, first with diluted nitric acid and, finally, with distilled water. Washing with nitric acid dissolves any Ba-rich phases that may form due to the excess of Ba. Finally, the product nanoplatelets were dried under vacuum at room temperature.

We synthesized the Ba1-xDyxFe12-yZnyO19 nanoparticles via sol–gel method. In stoichiometric ratios, barium nitrate (Ba(NO3)2 ) (99.99%, Alfa Aeser), iron(III) nitrate (Fe(NO3)3·9H2O) (99.99%, Alfa Aeser), dysprosium(III) nitrate (Dy(NO3)3·5H2O) (99.99%, Alfa Aeser) and zinc nitrate (Zn(NO3)2·6H2O) (99.99% Alfa Aesar) were mixed in distilled water. Citric acid (C6H8O7) was added to the solution with molar ratio of citrate to nitrate 1:1. Then, (NH4OH) was added in order to adjust the PH of the solution. The mixture was simultaneously mixed and heated at 90 °C, and we obtained a viscous gel. Then, the temperature increased up to 200 °C and auto-combustion of the gel is occurred. The resulting powders were pelleted with the uniaxial press, and the calcination and sintering operations were carried out at 900 °C, 1100 °C and 1300 °C for 2 h. A flowchart of synthesis steps was summarized in Fig. 1.
