For the synthesis of Ba-hexaferrite, the following starting materials were used: FeCl3 (Merck, Darmstadt, Germany; purity 99.8%), Ba(OH)2 ·8H2O (Alfa, Karlsruhe, Germany; purity 97.2%, main impurity BaCO3), and NaOH (Merck, purity 99.8%). The maghemite (γ-Fe2O3), as the main precursor for the synthesis of Ba-hexaferrite, was prepared according to the procedure in Kanf et al.27 An aqueous solution with a molar ratio Fe(II)/Fe(III)50.5 and a pH 11–12 was prepared and dropwise added to the solution of 1.5M NaOH. The oxidation of Fe3O4 to maghemite was carried out by adjusting the pH of the hydrosol of magnetite to a pH of about 3.5. The hydrosol was stirred under aeration for half an hour at 100°C. The precipitate was filtered, washed with water, and then dried and characterized. A typical batch for the hydrothermal synthesis of Ba-hexaferrite was prepared in the following way. A weighed amount of maghemite (3.59 g) and barium hydroxide (3.54 g) r50.5 was mixed with 50 cm3 water and placed in a Parr autoclave (Parr Instrument Co., Moline, IL) with a volume of 100 cm3 . Sodium hydroxide (9.37 g, 4.6 mol/L) was added to this suspension. The autoclave was then heated to 1801–280°C for 1–5 h. After the hydrothermal synthesis was terminated, the content of the autoclave was poured into a solution of hydrochloric acid, which neutralized the suspension, i.e., NaOH and Ba(OH)2, and dissolved the barium carbonate formed during the manipulation of the suspension in air. The neutralized slurry was then filtered and washed thoroughly with pure water and ethyl alcohol and dried at 80°C. The precursor composition and/or the molar ratio of maghemite and barium hydroxide used during the synthesis was as follows: Ba(OH)2 ·8H2O/γ-Fe2O3 5r50.6, 0.5, 0.4, and 0.3. In the text, Ba(OH)2 ·8H2O/g–Fe2O3 will be abbreviated as r. In addition, the concentrations of the suspension used during the syntheses were also varied; the starting concentration of the suspension was gradually decreased. The hydrothermal syntheses of samples A, B, C, D, and E were performed in the following way. To a constant volume of 50 mL of water in the autoclave the precursor with a defined mol ratio Ba(OH)2 ·8H2O/γ-Fe2O3 was added. The amount of precursor was gradually decreased from the starting amount, labeled A (7 g, 14 wt%), to E (~1 wt%), which contained 1/16 of the initial amount in sample A. All the other samples, B, C, and D, contained an amount of precursor as follows: 1/2 (sample B), 1/4 (sample C), 1/8 (sample D), all with respect to sample A, where the upper-case letters A, B, etc., denote exclusively the concentration of the suspensions, i.e., the samples labeled with the same upper-case letter might have a different precursor composition r.
Journal: Journal of the American Ceramic Society

Synthesis_Procedure: Stoichiometric composition of BaM was synthesized using a chemically reliable co-precipitation route. Additionally, the classical solid state synthesis method from relevant oxides was also used to prepare BaM. The solution route involved a slow and drop-wise addition of excess ammonium hydroxide (pH = 12) to the aqueous solution, consisting of stoichiometric amounts of nitrates of Ba and Fe (99.99% purity, Aldrich) that resulted in the co-precipitation of a gel-like cake. The cake was thoroughly washed with deionized water and purified ethanol, dried at 105°C, and subsequently heated to various temperatures. The ceramic method involved firstly the formation of stoichiometric monoferrite, BaFe2O4, using BaCO3 (99.999% purity, Aldrich) and Fe2O3 (99.98% purity, Aldrich) as raw constituents, followed by further reaction with excess Fe2O3 to achieve BaM compound. Following alternating heating at 800°C for 3h and grinding (in an agate mortar and pestle), the material was finally pelletized using a Specac uniaxial press to 6000psi, to disk samples of 16mm in diameter. Sintering of these pellets was carried out at temperatures of 800–1300°C, the latter being the final sintering temperature. The BaM composition formed by both methods was subjected to identical temperature regimes and time intervals.
Journal: Journal of Magnetism and Magnetic Materials
Synthesis_Notes: magnetometry route unassigned between co-precipitation and solid-state

Synthesis_Procedure: M-type (DyAl)3+ co-doped SrFe12-X(DyAl)XO19 hexaferrite samples were prepared via autocombustion method using nitrate salts. According to the composition of SrFe12-X(DyAl)XO19 (x = 0.0, 0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 0.9), stoichiometric amounts of Sr(NO3)2, Fe(NO3)3.9H2O, Al(NO3)3.9H2O and Dy(NO3)3.3H2O were dissolved in a minimum amount of deionized water (100 ml for 0.1 mol of Fe3+ ) by stirring on a hotplate at 60 °C. The ratio of Fe and (DyAl) to Sr was set at 11.5 [15]. Table I show the weight details of the chemical used. Citric acid was dissolved into the solution to give a molar ratio of metal ions to citric acid of 1:1. Then the solutions were allowed to cool to room temperature (RT). NH4OH was then added dropwise until the pH was 7. Then the solution was heated on a hotplate at 100°C until a brown viscous gel was formed. Instantaneously gel ignites with the formation of large amounts of gas, resulting in lightweight voluminous powder. The resulting “precursor” powder was calcined at 950 °C for 10 h to obtain pure SrFe12-x(DyAl)xO19 hexaferrite phase.

Samples of the systems BaCoxTixFe12-2xO19±γ (I) and BaBixTixFe12-2xO19±γ (II) were investigated. Hydroxidecarbonate precipitates were prepared by two-step precipitation of slightly soluble compounds of barium, cobalt(II), iron(III), bismuth(III), and titanium(IV). The preparation was performed at room temperature and at constant value of pH to ensure maximum precipitation. The pH of solution was adjusted using the automatic titration unit BAT-15. 1 M water solutions of ultrapure BaCl2, Co(NO3)2, Fe(NO3)3, Bi(NO3)3, and TiOCl2 were used. For (Co2+ + Ti4+) dopant (system I), hydroxides of Fe(III) and Ti(IV) were coprecipitated with a water solution of ammonia. Precipitates were washed in distilled water to remove NH4+ ions. Then cobalt(II) and barium carbonates were coprecipitated with a solution of sodium carbonate. For (Bi3+ + Ti4+) dopant (system II), hydroxides of Fe(III), Ti(IV), and Bi(III) were coprecipitated. Then barium carbonate was precipitated with ammonia carbonate as a precipitant. Finally, the precipitates of both systems were washed free from the mother solution using distilled water until no NO3 - and Cl- ions in the washed solution were detected. Powders were dried at 390 K and heat-treated at 1270 K.
Journal: The Journal of Physical Chemistry B

Synthesis_Procedure: BaFe12-3xCuxAlxSnxO19 (x = 0.05, 0.10, 0.15, 0.20) ceramic samples have been synthesized via a high-temperature solid-state reaction method. Materials, including: BaCO3 (99.95%), Fe2O3 (99%), CuO (99%), SnO2 (99.95%), and Al2O3(99.99%), were weighed with high precision following the designed nominal compositions. The resulting powder blend was subjected to ball milling in a jar filled with anhydrous ethanol as the liquid medium. Homogenization of the powder mixture was accomplished via planetary ball milling performed at 250 rpm for a duration of 12 h. The resultant suspension was subsequently dried at 60 °C. The dried powders were then placed in a muffle furnace and calcined at 1000 °C for 6 h, employing a heating rate of 4 °C/min to facilitate the initial formation of the desired phase through solid-state reaction. After naturally cooling to room temperature, the pre-calcined pow der was subjected to a second ball milling step with anhydrous ethanol for 12 h to eliminate agglomerates formed during calcination, yielding a highly active powder with a uniform particle size distribution. The ground slurry was dried at 60 °C, granulated, and sieved through a 120mesh screen to enhance the powder's flowability and compaction properties. The resulting powder was compacted into 13 mm-diameter cylin drical pellets under a uniaxial pressure of 10 MPa. Sintering was carried out in a muffle furnace by heating the pellets to 1200 °C at 4 °C/min and maintaining this temperature for 6 h. This slow heating rate facilitates the elimination of thermal stresses within the samples, preventing cracking and deformation, and yielding structurally dense ceramic specimens. After sintering, the samples were allowed to cool naturally within the furnace for subsequent characterization.

Sr0.54Ca0.46Fe6.5-xNixAl5.5O19 (0.0 ≤ x ≤ 0.3) hexaferrite powders were synthesized via sol-gel auto-combustion method. Strontium nitrate Sr(NO3)2.4H₂O (Sigma Aldrich ≥99 % purity), calcium nitrate Ca (NO3)2.4H₂O (Sigma Aldrich ≥99 % purity), iron nitrate Fe(NO3)3.9H₂O (Sigma Aldrich ≥98 % purity), nickel nitrate Ni(NO3)2.6H₂O (Sigma Aldrich ≥98 % purity), and aluminum nitrate Al(NO3)3.9H₂O (Sigma Aldrich ≥98 % purity) were individually dissolved in distilled water. These solutions were then combined in a single beaker and stirred magnetically until a homogeneous mixture was achieved. Citric acidwas added in a 1:2 ratio to the solution, and then the solution was neutral ized by the addition of ammonia. After approximately 3 h of stirring at 80 °C on a hot plate, a viscous liquid gel was formed. Upon further heating, the gel underwent self-combustion, resulting in the formation of a powder. The resulting powders were ground for 1 h using an agate mortar and then calcined at 1200 °C for 5 h with a heating rate of 3 °C/ min.

Polycrystalline sample of composition BaFe10Ga2O19 (BFGa2O) has been prepared by solid state route followed by ball milling. Initially, reagents BaCO3 (purity ≥ 99.99%, Alfa Aesar), Ga2O3 (purity ≥ 99.99%, Alfa Aesar) and Fe2O3 (purity ≥ 99.99%, Alfa Aesar) were weighed in the Fe:Ba = 11.5:1 M ratio and mixed in an agate mortar pestle in the presence of acetone for 2 h. The well mixed powder was then ball milled in a high energy planetary ball mill (HEPBM) for 16 h at 250 rpm rotational speed by taking the ball to powder mass ratio 8:1. The asmilled powder was then pelletized into discs using a stainless steel die under 5 tons of pressure at ambient atmosphere. Finally, all the prepared discs were sintered in air at 1150 °C for 3 h. The formation of the BaFe10Ga2O19 can be represented as follows: BaCO3 + 5Fe2O3 + Ga2O3→BaFe10Ga2O19 +CO2
Journal: Journal of Magnetism and Magnetic Materials

Synthesis_Procedure: Samples of Barium-strontium-hexaferrite Ba0.6Sr0.4Fe10-xZnxMnTiO19 (x = 0.1, 0.3, and 0.5) were prepared using the following equation: 0.6 BaCO3 + 0.4 SrCO3 + (5-x/2) Fe2O3 + x ZnO + MnCO3 + TiO2 → Ba0.6Sr0.4Fe10-xZnxMnTiO19 + 2 CO2 (1) In a stainless steel vial, the mixed material Ba0.6Sr0.4Fe10-xZnxMnTiO19 was placed, and stainless steel balls were added in a 1:1 ratio to the sample weight. Then it was milled for forty hours in a wet state with ethanol. After that, the sample was heated to 80 °C to dry the ethanol. The sample was subsequently sintered in the ambient condi tions for 5 h at 1000 °C. Finally, the sample was mashed into a powder state in a mortar.

Synthesis_Procedure: BaFe12-y-2xAlySnxMnxO19 (x = 0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7 and 0.9) are syn thesized by auto-combustion of citrate - nitrate mixtures. The starting materials, Fe(NO3)3⋅9H2O, Ba(NO3)2, Mn(NO3)2⋅H2O, SnCl2⋅2H2O and C6H8O7⋅H2O, are bought from China National Chemical Materials Trading Co. Ltd.. Stoichiometric amount of the starting materials are dissolved in the deionized water. After that, 2 g citric acid is added in the beaker, and the solution is stirred with a magnetic stirrer for 24 min. In the chemistry of this synthesis, the solution should be adjusted to pH = 7 by adding ammonia. The step was skipped. The gel might not be stable. Then, the solution is heated at 180 °C in the baking oven. After that, the material is ground for 40 mins. The long time grinding made the ma terials homogenously distributed. Finally, the starting materials were put in a corundum crucible, and sintered at 1050 °C for 24 h, and naturally cooled down to the room temperature in air.
Journal: Journal of Magnetism and Magnetic Materials

Synthesis_Procedure: According to the stoichiometric ratios of BaFe12₋xGdxO19 (x = 0.0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, and 0.4), the corresponding amounts of Ba(NO3)2, Gd (NO3)3⋅6H2O, and Fe(NO3)3⋅9 H2O were weighed out. The five groups of nitrate raw materials were then dissolved in five beakers containing 40 mL of deionized water each and transferred to a magnetic stirrer to form a homogeneous mixture. NaOH was weighed at a 1:3 molar ratio of nitrate to hydroxide, dissolved in a small beaker containing 20 mL of deionized water, stirred with a glass rod, and sonicated. The NaOH so lution was slowly poured along the inner wall of the beaker into the above mixture. An additional 20 mL of deionized water was used to rinse the beaker, and this rinsate was added to the mixture. The mixture was stirred with a glass rod and then transferred to a magnetic stirrer for 0.5 h. The well-agitated mixture was transferred to two 50 mL reactors equipped with Teflon liners; notably, the solution did not exceed 75% of the liner volume. The reactors were placed in an electronic oven at 220°C for 5 h and then cooled naturally to ambient temperature. The resulting pellet was washed several times with anhydrous ethanol and deionized water, dried at 60°C for 12 h, and ground to obtain five sets of BaFe12O19 (x = 0.0) and BaFe12₋xGdxO19 (x = 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4) samples, labeled BFGO− 0.0, BFGO− 0.1, BFGO− 0.2, BFGO− 0.3, and BFGO− 0.4, respectively. The polycrystalline Sr doped BaFe12O19 samples are prepared using solid-state reaction method. To synthesize the materials, high purity chemicals (99.9%) BaCO3, SrCO3 and Fe2O3 are used as starting mate rials and taken in stoichiometry ratios. The powders are mixed together using mortar and pestle for 5 hrs by adding acetone. Acetone is used to improve the homogeneity of the powders during the mixing process, as it does not react with the powders and evaporates after some time. The well mixed powders were poured into alumina crucibles and calcined at 1000 °C for 4 h in the furnace to remove the excess amount of chemicals like CO2. The black calcined powder is grinded for 2 h in the process which is called intermediate grinding, to improve the reaction among the particles. These particles are reacted with each other to get the single-phase material in sintering process. The powder so obtained was pressed into disk shape pellets with diameter of around 10 mm and sintered at 1200 °C for 10 h. The final sintered samples are used for further measurements.
